title: Portugal
blurb: History, places, food, music and nature of Portugal, from the Algarve to the Azores.

lessons.title: Portugal's geography
lessons.summary: Districts, regions, rivers and islands.

cards.title: Shape and size
cards.text: Mainland Portugal is a rectangle about 560 km long and 220 km wide. With the Azores and Madeira, the country covers about 92,000 km² and has around 10.6 million people.

deep.x: Mainland Portugal is a tall rectangle on the western edge of Iberia, from Melgaço in the north to Cabo de São Vicente in the south-west. Its Atlantic coast runs for over 900 km, and its land border with Spain, about 1,200 km, is one of the oldest unchanged frontiers in Europe.
How big is that?

Portugal is about a sixth of Spain's size, a little larger than Hungary and a little smaller than Austria. Driving from Valença to Faro takes about 6 hours by motorway. Of the total area, the mainland accounts for about 89,000 km², the Azores about 2,300 km² and Madeira about 800 km².
The edge of Europe

**Cabo da Roca**, near Sintra, is the westernmost point of mainland Europe, at about 9.5° W. The Azores island of Flores reaches even further west, about 31° W, making Portugal one of Europe's westernmost countries.

x: Population ≈ 10.6 million
Area ≈ 92,000 km²
Density ≈ 115 people per km²

deep.x: The poet Luís de Camões described Cabo da Roca as the place "where the land ends and the sea begins", words now carved on a monument there.
Portugal is a narrow strip of Atlantic coast plus two archipelagos far out at sea.

cards.title: Mainland and islands
cards.text: Portugal includes two autonomous regions in the Atlantic: the Azores (nine islands) and Madeira (Madeira, Porto Santo and uninhabited islets).

deep.x: The Azores and Madeira are **autonomous regions**: each has its own elected government and regional parliament, which handle matters like health, education, transport and tourism. Defence, foreign policy and justice stay with Lisbon. Autonomy came with the 1976 Constitution, after the 1974 revolution.
Nine Azorean islands

x: **Eastern group**: São Miguel (the largest, with Ponta Delgada) and Santa Maria
**Central group**: Terceira, Graciosa, São Jorge, Pico and Faial
**Western group**: Flores and Corvo

deep.x: The regional government sits in Ponta Delgada, the parliament in Horta and some departments in Angra do Heroísmo, a balance between the old rival islands.
Madeira's archipelago

Madeira island holds almost all the people. Porto Santo, 40 km away, has a long golden beach. The Desertas and the Selvagens are uninhabited nature reserves; the Selvagens lie closer to the Canary Islands than to Madeira.
Corvo, the smallest Azorean island, has only about 400 inhabitants, the least populous municipality in Portugal.
Portugal stretches into the Atlantic through two self-governing island regions.

cards.title: North and south
cards.text: The north is greener, more mountainous and densely populated near the coast; the south is flatter and drier, with the Alentejo's plains and the Algarve's beaches. The Tejo roughly divides them.

deep.x: The Tejo is a rough natural dividing line. North of it, the land is higher, wetter and rockier, mostly granite and schist. South of it, it's flatter, lower and drier, with rolling plains, cork oaks and wide wheat fields.
Land and history

The pattern runs deep. In the north, land was divided again and again among heirs, creating tiny plots called **minifúndios** and a dense scatter of villages and parishes. In the Alentejo, land reconquered from the Moors was granted in huge estates, the **latifúndios**, worked by landless labourers. After 1974 these estates were the scene of land occupations and agrarian reform.
Food follows the land

The north eats caldo verde, cabbage, chestnuts and vinho verde; the south bread soups (açordas), olive oil, pork from acorn-fed black pigs, and robust Alentejo reds. The Algarve's flatter coastal strip grows citrus and almonds and draws most of the tourists.
Over half of mainland Portugal's area lies south of the Tejo, but only about a third of its people live there.
North of the Tejo is green, hilly and crowded; south is flat, dry and spacious.

cards.title: Coast and interior
cards.text: Most people live near the coast between Viana do Castelo and Setúbal. The interior has been losing population for decades, a challenge for services and fire prevention.

deep.x: Portugal's population is pulled towards the sea. The coastal strip from Viana do Castelo to Setúbal, with the Lisbon and Porto metropolitan areas, holds the great majority of the people, the industry and the jobs. Inland districts like Bragança, Guarda, Castelo Branco and Portalegre have far fewer people than a century ago.
Why the interior emptied
From the 1960s, people left the interior for Lisbon, Porto and abroad. Today many inland parishes have more deaths than births and more than a third of residents aged 65 or over.
Fire and abandoned land

When fields are abandoned, scrub and fast-growing trees like eucalyptus and pine take over, and fewer people are around to clear them. This makes summer wildfires larger. The fires of June and October 2017 killed over 100 people and pushed fire prevention and rural policy to the top of the national agenda.

deep.w: Portugal's population is spread evenly
deep.r: Most people live within about 50 km of the coast

deep.x: Portugal leans towards the sea: busy coast, emptying interior.

cards.title: Regions of the mainland
cards.text: Common regions (NUTS II): Norte, Centro, Área Metropolitana de Lisboa, Alentejo and Algarve. Older provinces like Minho, Trás-os-Montes and Beira are still used in everyday speech.

deep.x: Portugal has several overlapping maps. The 18 mainland **districts** date from 1835 and are still used for many purposes, such as car-free civil protection and football associations. The **NUTS II regions** are an EU statistical system, used to share out EU funds. And the old **provinces** live on in everyday speech and identity.

items: Alentejo (incl. Oeste e Vale do Tejo)

deep.x: The old provinces

People still say they're from the Minho, Trás-os-Montes, the Beira, the Ribatejo or the Alentejo. These traditional provinces were formally defined in 1936 and abolished as administrative units in 1976, but they still describe landscapes, accents, food and folklore better than any official map.
Municipalities and parishes

The units that run daily life are the **308 municípios** (councils) and their **freguesias** (parishes), around 3,000 of them. Portugal has no elected regional governments on the mainland; a 1998 referendum on creating them was rejected.
In 2024 the NUTS II map was redrawn: Lisbon split into Grande Lisboa and the Península de Setúbal, and Oeste and the Tejo valley moved into the Centro and Alentejo regions.
Districts, NUTS regions and provinces all coexist; the old provinces still define identity.

cards.title: The Minho

items: Ponte de Lima, Portugal's oldest town charter (1125)

cards.text: The Minho, in the far northwest, is green and rainy, known for vinho verde, granite villages, the Lima and Minho rivers, and towns like Viana do Castelo, Ponte de Lima and Braga.

deep.x: The Minho, Portugal's north-western corner, sits between the Minho and Douro rivers and faces straight into Atlantic storms. Its mild, wet climate makes it the greenest region in the country, a landscape of maize fields, vines on pergolas, granite walls and hillsides of oak and pine.
Vinho verde

"Green wine" refers to youth, not colour. It's light, fresh and often slightly sparkling, made from grapes like Alvarinho (especially around Monção and Melgaço) and Loureiro. Vines were traditionally trained high on trees and pergolas so that crops like maize and beans could grow below.
Culture and tradition

The Minho is known for **espigueiros** (granite granaries on stilts), the gold filigree and traditional costumes of Viana, and the Romaria d'Agonia in August. Ponte de Lima, with its medieval bridge, claims to be Portugal's oldest town, chartered in 1125.
Many espigueiros in Soajo and Lindoso, near Peneda-Gerês, are still used today and some are over 200 years old.
The Minho is Portugal's green, rainy, granite north-west, the land of vinho verde.

cards.title: Peneda-Gerês
cards.text: Portugal's only national park, created in 1971, protects granite mountains, oak forests, wild Garrano horses, wolves and traditional villages along the Spanish border.

deep.x: The **Parque Nacional da Peneda-Gerês** covers about 700 km² in the far north, along the border with Galicia, where it joins Spain's Baixa Limia–Serra do Xurés park. It includes the Peneda, Soajo, Amarela and Gerês mountains, reaching 1,548 m.
Wild residents

The **Garrano** is a small, sturdy native horse that roams semi-wild in the hills. The park is a stronghold for the Iberian wolf, protected in Portugal since 1988, and for rare plants like the Gerês lily.
People in the park

Unlike many national parks, this one includes inhabited villages. Places like Soajo, Lindoso and Pitões das Júnias keep traditions such as communal grazing and the **brandas and inverneiras** system, where families moved between summer pastures up high and winter homes in the valleys. A Roman road, the Geira, crosses the park with many milestones still standing.
The ruined village of Vilarinho da Furna was flooded by a dam in 1972; in dry summers its stone walls reappear from the reservoir.
Portugal's only national park protects wild granite mountains and the villages that shaped them.

cards.title: Rivers and dams
cards.text: Portugal's big rivers have many dams for hydropower and water storage. The Alqueva reservoir on the Guadiana, completed in 2002, is one of Western Europe's largest artificial lakes.

deep.x: Portugal has over 250 large dams. They store water from wet winters for dry summers, generate electricity and supply irrigation and drinking water. Some also help control floods. Most big hydroelectric dams are on the Douro, Cávado, Tejo and Zêzere.
Alqueva

The **Alqueva** dam on the Guadiana, closed in 2002, created a reservoir of about 250 km², one of the largest artificial lakes in Western Europe, with a shoreline over 1,000 km long. Its water irrigates over 120,000 hectares of the Alentejo, transforming dry farmland into olive groves, almond orchards and vineyards.
Costs and benefits

Dams flood valleys, villages and farmland, block fish migration and trap sediment that would otherwise feed beaches. The old village of Aldeia da Luz was rebuilt elsewhere for Alqueva. Hydropower is still a big part of Portugal's renewable electricity, varying from about 10% in dry years to 30% in wet ones, and some dams pump water back uphill to store wind and solar energy.
Dams let Portugal save winter rain for summer, at a cost to rivers and the coast.

cards.title: The Azores
cards.text: The Azores lie about 1,400 km west of Lisbon on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. They're volcanic, green and famous for crater lakes, hot springs, whales and tea plantations.

deep.x: The Azores lie about 1,400 km west of Lisbon, roughly a third of the way to North America. They grew from volcanoes along the **Mid-Atlantic Ridge**, at the meeting point of three tectonic plates, and they're still geologically active: earthquakes are common and some islands have hot springs and fumaroles.
Mild, wet and green

The climate is oceanic: mild all year (around 14–24 °C), humid and changeable, often with "four seasons in one day". The high pressure that forms in the region, the **Azores High**, shapes weather across Europe, bringing settled summers to Portugal.
Volcanic living

x: In Furnas, the **cozido das Furnas** stew is cooked for hours in pots buried in hot volcanic ground.
Pico's vineyards grow inside black lava walls, a UNESCO World Heritage landscape since 2004.
Gorreana on São Miguel is Europe's oldest tea plantation still working, since 1883.

deep.x: Former whaling lookouts (vigias) on Pico and Faial now guide whale-watching boats; about a third of the world's whale and dolphin species have been seen in Azorean waters.
The Azores are green volcanoes in mid-Atlantic, sitting where three plates meet.

cards.title: Madeira
cards.text: Madeira, about 1,000 km southwest of Lisbon, is a steep volcanic island with laurel forests (UNESCO), levadas (irrigation channels with walking paths) and its famous fortified wine.

deep.x: Madeira lies about 1,000 km south-west of Lisbon and about 600 km from Africa's coast. It's the top of a huge volcanic shield rising from the ocean floor, so steep that much of the island seems to stand on end. Its peaks reach 1,862 m at Pico Ruivo.
The laurel forest

The **Laurissilva** is a forest of laurel-type trees that once covered much of southern Europe millions of years ago. Madeira holds the largest surviving area, about 15,000 hectares, listed by UNESCO in 1999. It catches moisture from clouds and feeds the island's springs.
Levadas

Most rain falls on the wet north side, while farms and towns cluster on the sunnier south. From the 1500s, Madeirans cut **levadas**, narrow channels, into cliffs to carry water around the mountains. There are over 2,000 km of them, and the maintenance paths beside them are now famous walking trails.
Madeira wine

Madeira wine is fortified and then heated. Merchants found that casks carried through the tropics on ships improved, so producers began warming the wine on purpose. The result can last for well over a century.
Madeira's island records include Cristiano Ronaldo, born in Funchal in 1985, whose name is now on the island's airport.
Madeira is a steep volcanic garden, watered by ancient forest and hand-cut channels.

quiz.explain: Completed in 2002.

lessons.title: The birth of Portugal
lessons.summary: From county to kingdom, and the battle that saved it.

cards.title: The County of Portucale
cards.text: Portugal began as a county of the kingdom of León, named after Portucale, today's Porto area. In 1096 it was given to Henry of Burgundy and his wife Teresa.

deep.x: The name **Portucale** joined two places on the Douro: Portus (a port on the north bank, today's Porto) and Cale (on the south bank, near Gaia). In 868 a nobleman, Vímara Peres, took the area back from Muslim control and it became a county, a territory run by a count for the king of León.
Henry and Teresa

Around 1096 King Alfonso VI of León and Castile gave the county to **Henry of Burgundy**, a French knight who had come to fight the Muslims. Henry married Teresa, Alfonso's daughter (born outside marriage). The county stretched roughly from the Minho to around Coimbra.
Teresa rules alone

Henry died in 1112. Teresa ruled the county and called herself "queen". She grew close to a powerful Galician noble, Fernão Peres de Trava, which worried Portuguese barons who feared being swallowed by Galicia.

deep.w: Portugal was founded by a Portuguese hero against foreigners
deep.r: Its founders were a French count and a Leonese princess, and the early fight was a family and noble power struggle

deep.x: Portugal began as a frontier county on the Douro, granted by one king to a foreign knight.

cards.title: São Mamede, 1128
cards.text: Young Afonso Henriques defeated his mother Teresa's forces at the Battle of São Mamede near Guimarães in 1128, taking control of the county. Guimarães is called "the cradle of Portugal".

deep.x: On 24 June 1128, near Guimarães, the young **Afonso Henriques**, then about 17–20 years old, beat the forces of his mother Teresa and her ally Fernão Peres de Trava. Teresa left for Galicia, where she died two years later.
Why it mattered
It was a modest battle, but it put power in the hands of a ruler backed by the local nobility. From then on Afonso pushed for independence from León and expansion south against the Muslims.
The cradle

Guimarães was the county's main seat. Its castle and the Palace of the Dukes of Braganza sit on the "sacred hill", and a section of the old town wall bears the words "Aqui nasceu Portugal", "Portugal was born here".

x: Afonso's exact birth year and place are uncertain; Guimarães, Viseu and Coimbra all claim him
Tradition says he was baptised in the small church of São Miguel by the castle

deep.x: A later legend says Afonso even chained up his mother; it's a chroniclers' story with little evidence.
At São Mamede a son beat his mother, and a county started on the road to being a kingdom.

cards.title: Recognition: 1143 and 1179
cards.text: At the Treaty of Zamora (1143), Alfonso VII of León recognised Afonso as king. The Pope formally confirmed it in 1179 with the bull Manifestis Probatum.

deep.x: Medieval kingdoms needed recognition. After victories such as **Ourique** (1139), Afonso began calling himself king. In 1143, at Zamora, his cousin Alfonso VII of León, who called himself "emperor of Spain", accepted Afonso's royal title, with a papal envoy present.
Going over León's head

Afonso then declared himself a vassal of the Pope and promised an annual tribute of gold. This was clever: owing loyalty directly to Rome meant not owing it to León. The Popes delayed for decades, but in 1179 Alexander III issued the bull **Manifestis Probatum**, calling Afonso king and his land a kingdom.
Why the Pope agreed
Afonso had proved useful: he had taken Lisbon and pushed far south against Muslim rulers, which the Church saw as a crusade. Money and military success made the case.
The Treaty of Zamora is traditionally dated 5 October 1143, the same day of the year the Portuguese Republic was proclaimed in 1910.
Portugal became a kingdom in two steps: a neighbour's nod in 1143 and the Pope's seal in 1179.

cards.title: Moving south
cards.text: Afonso and his successors took Santarém and Lisbon (1147), then the Alentejo and finally the Algarve (1249). Portugal's borders, set by the Treaty of Alcañices in 1297, are among Europe's oldest.

deep.x: Expansion was both conquest and settlement. Kings granted land and charters (forais) to attract settlers, and military orders such as the Templars, Hospitallers and Order of Santiago held frontier castles.
Lisbon, 1147

Santarém fell to a surprise night attack in March 1147. That summer, a fleet of crusaders from England, Flanders and Germany, sailing to the Holy Land, stopped in Porto and agreed to help. After a siege of about 17 weeks, Lisbon surrendered in October. The crusaders were paid in plunder, and some stayed.
Setbacks
In 1169 Afonso was wounded and captured at Badajoz, and the Almohads fought back hard in the 1190s. It took four more kings to reach the coast of the Algarve: Afonso III took Faro in 1249.
Fixed borders

In 1297 King Dinis and Castile signed the Treaty of Alcañices. Portugal gained the Riba-Côa area, and the land border has barely moved since, apart from the disputed town of Olivença, taken by Spain in 1801.
Portugal's land border with Spain is about 1,200 km long and one of the oldest stable borders in Europe.
In about 150 years Portugal reached the south coast, and then kept the same shape for more than seven centuries.

cards.title: King Dinis
cards.text: Dom Dinis (reigned 1279–1325) planted the pine forest of Leiria to protect farmland and supply timber, founded the university, made Portuguese the official language of documents and created the Order of Christ.

deep.x: Dom Dinis came to the throne in 1279 at 17. With the reconquest finished, he could focus on building the country. He was nicknamed **o Lavrador**, "the Farmer", and also "the Poet King".
Order of Christ

When the Pope dissolved the Templars in 1312, many kings seized their wealth. Dinis instead created a new order, the **Order of Christ**, in 1319, and handed it the Templars' castles and lands. A century later its money would help pay for Henry the Navigator's voyages, and its red cross flew on the sails.
Land and sea

He set up fairs, protected farmers, rebuilt dozens of castles along the border and hired a Genoese admiral, Manuel Pessanha, in 1317 to organise a navy. The pine forest near Leiria held back moving sand dunes and later supplied timber for ships.
A poet king
Dinis wrote more than 130 songs (cantigas) in Galician-Portuguese, many of them love songs in a woman's voice. His wife, Isabel of Aragon, became a saint, the Rainha Santa of Coimbra.
About 86% of the Pinhal de Leiria burned in the fires of October 2017; replanting is still under way.
Dinis turned a conquered territory into a working kingdom with its own language, schools and forests.

cards.title: The 1383–85 crisis
cards.text: When King Fernando died without a son, Castile claimed the throne. Many Portuguese backed João, Master of Avis. The crisis became a fight for independence.

deep.x: King Fernando died in October 1383. His only heir was his daughter **Beatriz**, aged about 10 and married to Juan I of Castile. If she inherited, Portugal could become part of Castile. Fernando's widow, Leonor Teles, ruled as regent, influenced by a Galician noble, Count Andeiro.
Who backed whom

In December 1383 João, Master of the military Order of Avis and Fernando's half-brother born outside marriage, killed Andeiro in the palace. Lisbon's people rose in support. Much of the high nobility, however, sided with Castile.
Holding on

Castile besieged Lisbon by land and sea in 1384, but plague broke out in its camp and the army withdrew. Meanwhile the young commander Nuno Álvares Pereira won at Atoleiros in the Alentejo. In April 1385 the Cortes in Coimbra chose João as king, after the lawyer João das Regras argued that the throne was vacant.
Most of what we know comes from Fernão Lopes, a royal chronicler writing about 50 years later, who gave unusual attention to ordinary townspeople.
The crisis turned a succession quarrel into the first moment of Portuguese national identity.

cards.title: Aljubarrota, 1385
cards.text: On 14 August 1385, a smaller Portuguese army under Nuno Álvares Pereira and King João I, with English archers, defeated Castile at Aljubarrota using defensive tactics. Independence was secured.

deep.x: Juan I of Castile invaded with a large army, including heavy French cavalry. João I and Nuno Álvares chose to wait for them on ground they had picked, near Aljubarrota, between Leiria and Alcobaça.
Defensive tactics

The Portuguese stood on foot on a small plateau, with streams protecting the flanks. In front they dug ditches and hidden pits, and English archers shot from the sides. These were the same ideas the English used against the French at Crécy and Poitiers.

The Castilian army arrived tired, late in the afternoon of 14 August, and attacked a narrow front. Charging knights fell into the ditches and were cut down. Juan I fled to Santarém and then by sea to Seville.

deep.w: Brites de Almeida killed seven Castilians with her baker's shovel
deep.r: It's a much-loved later legend, not a documented event

deep.x: Numbers for both armies are estimates from chroniclers; historians agree only that Portugal was heavily outnumbered.
At Aljubarrota good ground and discipline beat sheer numbers, and Portugal stayed independent.

cards.title: Batalha monastery
cards.text: João I built the Monastery of Santa Maria da Vitória at Batalha to give thanks for Aljubarrota. It's a UNESCO World Heritage site and a masterpiece of Gothic and Manueline art.

deep.x: João I had vowed to build a monastery to the Virgin if he won. Work began in 1386 at a site a few kilometres from the battlefield, and the town that grew around it took the name **Batalha**, simply "battle".
Highlights

The Chapter House roof is a star vault about 19 m across with no central support. Legend says the architect, Afonso Domingues, now blind, sat under it for three days to prove it would not fall. It now holds the tomb of Portugal's Unknown Soldiers from the First World War, with a guard of honour.
Unfinished forever

King Duarte began a second burial chapel, but later kings moved their money and attention to the Jerónimos in Lisbon. So the Unfinished Chapels still stand open to the sky, with huge carved Manueline doorways.
Henry the Navigator and his brothers lie in the Founder's Chapel, beside their parents.
Batalha is a battle turned into stone: a thank-you that took more than a century to build.

cards.title: The oldest alliance

events.l: João I marries Philippa of Lancaster

cards.text: The Treaty of Windsor (1386) between Portugal and England is the oldest diplomatic alliance in the world still in force. João I married Philippa of Lancaster, mother of Prince Henry the Navigator.

deep.x: Portugal and England first made an alliance in 1373. After Aljubarrota, where English archers had fought, they signed the **Treaty of Windsor** on 9 May 1386, promising "perpetual friendship" and mutual help.
A royal marriage

In 1387 João I married **Philippa of Lancaster**, daughter of John of Gaunt, in Porto Cathedral. She brought English courtiers and customs. Their children, later called the "Ínclita Geração" (illustrious generation), included King Duarte, Prince Pedro and Prince Henry.
Using it
The alliance had rough patches, like Britain's 1890 ultimatum over African territory, which caused outrage in Portugal. But it has been invoked many times.
In 1943 neutral Portugal let the Allies use bases in the Azores, citing the old alliance; the Lajes base is still used by the US today.
A treaty signed after a medieval battle still links Lisbon and London more than 600 years later.

cards.title: The Avis dynasty
cards.text: The Avis kings launched the overseas expansion: Ceuta (1415), the Atlantic islands, the African coast and finally India. It was the start of Portugal's golden age.

deep.x: The House of Avis ruled from 1385 to 1580. With peace with Castile signed in 1411, Portugal's kings, short of land to conquer at home, looked overseas for gold, trade and crusading glory.
Why go?

Ceuta, captured in 1415, was a rich Moroccan port. It turned out to be costly to hold, but it showed what the sea could offer. Henry the Navigator then sponsored voyages down Africa's coast, and Madeira and the Azores were settled. A darker side began early: by the 1440s Portuguese ships were bringing enslaved Africans to Lagos.
The end

The dynasty ended in tragedy. King Sebastião died at Alcácer Quibir in Morocco in 1578, without an heir. His elderly great-uncle, Cardinal Henrique, reigned briefly, and in 1580 Philip II of Spain took the throne.

deep.w: Henry the Navigator ran a school of navigation at Sagres
deep.r: He rarely went to sea himself, and the "school of Sagres" is a later myth; he organised and paid for voyages

deep.x: The Avis kings turned a small kingdom into the first global sea power.

quiz.explain: The Portuguese, with English allies.

lessons.title: Portugal and the Age of Discovery
lessons.summary: How a small kingdom at the edge of Europe opened the world's sea routes.

cards.title: Why Portugal turned to the sea
cards.text:
In the 1400s Portugal was small, poor and boxed in by Castile. The rich trade in spices and silk came overland from Asia and was controlled by Venice and Muslim middlemen.

The Atlantic was the one open door. Prince Henry 'the Navigator' sponsored expeditions down the African coast, step by step, hoping to reach gold, allies and eventually the spices of India by sea.

deep.x: Portugal had perhaps a million people in the 1400s, poor soils in much of the country and a long land border with a much bigger Castile. Expansion by land was blocked. But it had a long Atlantic coast, skilled fishermen, and Lisbon, a busy port where Genoese and other merchants brought money and know-how.
The motives

West African gold reached Europe through Muslim traders across the Sahara. Reaching it by sea would cut out the middlemen. Europeans also hoped to find "Prester John", a legendary Christian king in Africa or Asia, as an ally against Islam.
Step by step
The capture of Ceuta, a North African port, gave Portugal's nobles a taste for overseas ventures. Islands like Madeira soon paid for themselves with wheat and then sugar, funding further voyages.

x: Peace with Castile from 1411 freed resources for adventures abroad
Royal support meant voyages could continue for decades

deep.x: Cape Bojador, on today's Western Sahara coast, was feared as a point of no return. Gil Eanes finally sailed past it in 1434 and found the sea beyond was perfectly ordinary.
Portugal went to sea not because it was strong, but because the ocean was the one direction it could grow.

cards.title: The caravel
cards.text:
Square sails work beautifully with the wind behind you, but badly against it. The caravel's triangular 'lateen' sails let it sail much closer into the wind, and its shallow hull could explore coasts and rivers.

That mattered: coming home from West Africa meant fighting the prevailing winds. Explorers learned to swing far out into the Atlantic to catch better ones.

deep.x: The caravel was a small, light ship, typically 20–25 metres long with a crew of about 20. Its **lateen** sails, triangular and set along the length of the ship, came from Mediterranean and Arab sailing traditions.
The return problem

Sailing south along Africa was easy: the trade winds blew that way. Coming back meant beating against them for weeks. The solution was the **volta do mar** ("turn of the sea"): sail far out into the open Atlantic, curve north to the latitude of the Azores, and ride the westerly winds home.
Shallow and nimble
A shallow hull let caravels creep along unknown coasts, enter river mouths and avoid sandbanks. They were less useful for heavy cargo, so later fleets mixed caravels with bigger ships.

x: Columbus' Niña and Pinta were caravels
The "caravela redonda" added square sails for speed downwind
Da Gama's fleet to India used larger naus plus one caravel, the Bérrio

deep.w: Caravels carried the spice trade
deep.r: They were exploration ships; the cargo was carried by big naus (carracks) able to hold hundreds of tonnes

deep.x: The caravel's genius was not size but agility: it could go into the wind and into the unknown.

cards.title: Finding latitude from the stars
cards.text:
On open water there are no landmarks. In the northern hemisphere, the height of the Pole Star above the horizon roughly equals your latitude. Sailors measured it with a quadrant or astrolabe.

Further south the Pole Star disappears, so Portuguese navigators measured the Sun at noon instead and used printed tables to correct for the season.

deep.x: Latitude is how far north or south of the equator you are. Because Earth is round, the sky looks different at different latitudes. At the North Pole, the Pole Star is overhead (90°); at the equator it sits on the horizon (0°). In between, its height above the horizon matches your latitude.
Using the Sun instead

Below the equator, the Pole Star disappears. The Sun is always there, but its noon height changes with the seasons. Portuguese astronomers produced tables of the Sun's **declination**: how far north or south of the equator it is on each day.

x: 21 June, Sun at noon is 74.7° high
Table says declination = +23.4°
90 − 74.7 + 23.4 = 38.7° N, the latitude of Lisbon

deep.x: The instruments

items.b: heavy brass ring, sights the Sun

deep.x: Tables printed in the 1490s, including Abraham Zacuto's almanac, published in Leiria in 1496, made the method reliable.
What they couldn't do

Longitude, your east–west position, needed accurate time at sea. That problem wasn't solved until marine chronometers in the late 1700s. Until then, navigators sailed to the right latitude and then ran east or west along it.
In the 1400s the Pole Star was about 3.5° away from the true pole, so pilots learned a rule, the "regimento do Norte", to correct for its position.
A simple angle, measured with care and corrected with tables, told sailors where they were on an empty ocean.

cards.title: The great voyages
cards.text:
Bartolomeu Dias rounded the southern tip of Africa in 1488. Ten years later Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in India, opening the sea route to the spice trade and making Lisbon one of Europe's richest ports.

In 1500 Pedro Álvares Cabral, heading for India, swung so far west that he reached Brazil. And Fernão de Magalhães (Magellan), a Portuguese sailing for Spain, led the first voyage around the world, completed by Elcano in 1522.
cards.sketch: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g class="d"><path class="a" d="M20 92L300 92"/><circle class="fred" cx="40" cy="92" r="6"/><circle class="fred" cx="100" cy="92" r="6"/><circle class="fred" cx="160" cy="92" r="6"/><circle class="fred" cx="220" cy="92" r="6"/><circle class="fred" cx="280" cy="92" r="6"/></g><text class="r" x="40" y="76" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:18px">1419</text><text class="" x="40" y="116" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:15px">Madeira</text><text class="" x="40" y="134" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:15px"></text><text class="r" x="100" y="76" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:18px">1488</text><text class="" x="100" y="116" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:15px">Dias:</text><text class="" x="100" y="134" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:15px">Good Hope</text><text class="r" x="160" y="76" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:18px">1498</text><text class="" x="160" y="116" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:15px">da Gama:</text><text class="" x="160" y="134" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:15px">India</text><text class="r" x="220" y="76" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:18px">1500</text><text class="" x="220" y="116" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:15px">Cabral:</text><text class="" x="220" y="134" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:15px">Brazil</text><text class="r" x="280" y="76" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:18px">1522</text><text class="" x="280" y="116" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:15px">round the</text><text class="" x="280" y="134" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:15px">world</text><text class="" x="160" y="168" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:14px">not to scale</text></svg>

deep.x: Each voyage built on the one before. Pilots, maps and wind knowledge were carefully gathered in Lisbon and often kept secret from rivals.
Dias and da Gama

Bartolomeu Dias was blown south by a storm and only realised he had passed Africa's tip when he turned north and found the coast on his left. He called it the Cape of Storms; the king renamed it the Cape of Good Hope. Vasco da Gama left Lisbon in July 1497 with four ships and took about ten months to reach Calicut. He made a huge loop through the South Atlantic, months without sight of land. Many of his men died of scurvy; perhaps a third returned in 1499.
Cabral and Magellan

Cabral's fleet of 13 ships landed at Porto Seguro in April 1500, then continued to India. Fernão de Magalhães, after a quarrel with King Manuel I, offered his services to Spain. He found the strait at South America's tip that bears his name, crossed the Pacific, and was killed in the Philippines in 1521. Juan Sebastián Elcano brought the last ship home.
Magellan named the Pacific ("peaceful") because his crossing met calm weather; it is the largest ocean on Earth.
In 34 years, Portuguese navigators turned the edge of the known world into a set of sea routes.

cards.title: Splitting the world: Tordesillas
cards.text:
In 1494 Portugal and Castile signed the Treaty of Tordesillas, drawing a line from pole to pole 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde islands. New lands to the west would go to Castile, to the east to Portugal.

The tip of South America that bulged east of the line became Brazil, which is a big part of why around 210 million Brazilians speak Portuguese today.
cards.sketch: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g class="d"><circle class="s bgf" cx="160" cy="98" r="64"/><ellipse class="dash" cx="160" cy="98" rx="32" ry="64"/><path class="dash" d="M96 98L224 98"/><path class="r" d="M136 26L136 172"/></g><text class="" x="62" y="70" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:17px">Castile</text><text class="a" x="262" y="70" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:17px">Portugal</text><text class="a" x="160" y="136" text-anchor="start" style="font-size:15px">Brazil</text><text class="r" x="12" y="22" text-anchor="start" style="font-size:20px">1494</text><text class="r" x="308" y="22" text-anchor="end" style="font-size:13px">370 leagues W of Cape Verde</text></svg>

deep.x: After Columbus returned in 1493, the Pope issued a bull giving Castile lands west of a line 100 leagues beyond the Azores and Cape Verde. King João II of Portugal protested and negotiated directly with Castile, moving the line much further west.

x: 370 leagues west of Cape Verde
leagues varied, so about 2,000 km
line at roughly 46° W, cutting through today's Brazil

deep.x: Why move the line?

Historians debate whether Portugal already suspected land in the west. Either way, the wider sea gave room for the Atlantic loop on the way to India, and it put Brazil's eastern bulge on Portugal's side.
What happened next

x: Other powers like France, England and the Netherlands ignored the treaty
Portuguese settlers and explorers pushed far west of the line into the Amazon
The Treaty of Madrid in 1750 accepted borders close to Brazil's modern ones

deep.w: The Pope divided the world between Spain and Portugal
deep.r: The final line came from a direct treaty between the two crowns; the Pope later confirmed it

deep.x: A line drawn on a map in a small Castilian town decided the language of half of South America.

cards.title: Prince Henry's role
cards.text: Infante D. Henrique (1394–1460) didn't sail far himself, but he organised and funded voyages down the African coast from the Algarve, gathering pilots, mapmakers and shipbuilders.

deep.x: D. Henrique was the third surviving son of King João I and Philippa of Lancaster. He fought at Ceuta in 1415 and became governor of the Order of Christ, a wealthy military-religious order whose income helped pay for ships.

items.b: Order of Christ and trade rights

deep.x: What he achieved

Under his sponsorship, expeditions colonised Madeira and the Azores, passed Cape Bojador and reached as far as Sierra Leone by the time he died in 1460. He held monopolies on trade along the coast and took a share of the profits.
The myth of Sagres

items.r: An organiser who rarely sailed far

deep.x: A complicated figure
His ventures also began the Portuguese trade in enslaved Africans: in 1444 captives were sold at Lagos, watched by Henry himself. He was also behind the disastrous attack on Tangier in 1437.
The nickname "the Navigator" was popularised by English and German writers in the 1800s; Portuguese sources usually just call him the Infante.
Henry's real invention was persistence: decades of funded, step-by-step voyages instead of one heroic gamble.

cards.title: The spice trade

steps: Spices in India and the Moluccas

cards.text: Pepper, cinnamon, cloves and nutmeg were worth fortunes in Europe. The sea route to India let Portugal buy at the source, bypassing Venetian and Middle Eastern middlemen.

deep.x: In medieval Europe, spices were luxuries and status symbols. Pepper came from India's Malabar coast, cinnamon from Sri Lanka, and cloves and nutmeg only from a few tiny islands in today's Indonesia.
The old route
At each stage, a merchant or ruler took a cut, so prices multiplied many times on the way. Venice grew rich as the main European buyer.
The Cape route

The voyage was dangerous; ships and lives were often lost. But one successful fleet could pay for several failures. The crown controlled imports through the Casa da Índia in Lisbon, and pepper became the state's great business.

x: Lisbon became Europe's pepper market in the early 1500s
Venice's trade fell sharply at first but partly recovered later
From about 1600 the Dutch and English pushed Portugal aside

deep.w: Spices were used to hide rotten meat
deep.r: Those who could afford spices could afford fresh meat; spices were about flavour, medicine and prestige

deep.x: The spice trade was about cutting out middlemen, and whoever controlled the sea route controlled the profit.

cards.title: The Portuguese in Asia
cards.text: Portugal built a network of trading posts and forts: Goa (1510), Malacca (1511), Hormuz and later Macau (1557). Portuguese traders were the first Europeans to reach Japan, in 1543.

deep.x: Portugal couldn't conquer Asia's great empires. Instead, governor Afonso de Albuquerque seized a few key ports to control the main sea lanes, creating the **Estado da Índia**, a network of forts, trading posts and fleets.
How it worked

Goa was the capital. Malacca controlled the strait to the spice islands, Hormuz the entrance to the Persian Gulf. Portugal forced local ships to buy passes, called **cartazes**, and attacked those without them. It was a sea empire run by violence as well as trade.
Long-lasting traces
In Japan, Portuguese traders brought firearms, which spread rapidly, and Jesuit missionaries converted many people before Christianity was banned in the early 1600s.

deep.w: Japanese "arigatō" comes from "obrigado"
deep.r: The Japanese word existed before the Portuguese arrived; it's a coincidence

deep.x: Tempura is often linked to Portuguese missionaries' meatless fasting days ("tempora"), though the exact origin is debated.
Portugal's Asian empire was a chain of ports, not territory, and its traces are still in Asian food, words and families.

cards.title: The dark side

items: Abolished in Portugal's empire in stages in the 1800s

cards.text: The voyages also opened the Atlantic slave trade. Over three and a half centuries, Portuguese and Brazilian ships carried more enslaved Africans across the Atlantic than any other nation's, a history now studied and acknowledged.

deep.x: The Portuguese began trading enslaved people from West Africa in the 1440s. After sugar plantations spread to the Atlantic islands and then Brazil, the trade grew enormously. Enslaved Africans were forced across the ocean in brutal conditions; many died on the way.
The scale
In total about 12.5 million people were forced onto ships from Africa between the 1500s and 1860s, and about 10.7 million survived the crossing. Brazil received the largest share, about 4.8 million.
Ending it
Brazil was the last country in the Americas to abolish slavery. The legacy lives on in Brazil's population, culture and inequalities, and in African communities shaped by the trade.

x: Lagos opened a museum on the site of its old slave market in 2016
Lisbon has planned a memorial to the enslaved people

deep.x: Estimates come from the Slave Voyages database, built by historians from records of more than 36,000 voyages.
The same ships that connected the world also carried the largest forced migration in history.

cards.title: Legacy of the discoveries
cards.text: The voyages connected continents, spread crops (maize, potatoes, tomatoes to Europe; sugar, coffee to the Americas), languages and diseases, and began globalisation, with both benefits and great suffering.

deep.x: The voyages started an exchange of plants, animals, people and germs between continents that had been separate for millennia, often called the **Columbian Exchange**.
Winners and losers

New crops helped Europe's and Asia's populations grow. But diseases like smallpox and measles, to which Indigenous Americans had no immunity, killed a huge share of the population, in some regions perhaps up to 90%.
Portugal's part

Portuguese traders carried chillies from Brazil to India and Asia within decades, so curries and Thai food owe something to them. They also brought tea to Europe's attention and spread words, foods and Christianity.

x: The Portuguese language spread to Brazil, Africa and Asia
Mixed communities and creole languages formed in Cabo Verde, Goa and Macau
Global trade networks began linking every inhabited continent

deep.x: In Greek, Turkish and Arabic, the word for orange sounds like "Portugal" (portokáli, portakal, burtuqāl), because Portuguese traders spread the sweet orange.
The discoveries made the world one connected system, with gifts and catastrophes travelling along the same routes.

quiz.q: What could a caravel do better than a square-rigged ship?
options: Sail faster with the wind behind
quiz.explain: Its lateen sails let it work into the wind, essential for exploring and getting home.

quiz.q: Who first reached India by sea from Europe?
quiz.explain: Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in 1498.

quiz.q: Why does Brazil speak Portuguese?
options: Cabral claimed it and it lay on Portugal's side of the Tordesillas line
quiz.explain: Cabral landed in 1500, and the land fell east of the 1494 treaty line.

quiz.q: Where was Portugal's main base in India?
quiz.explain: Goa was taken in 1510.

quiz.q: Who were the first Europeans to reach Japan, in 1543?
quiz.explain: Portuguese traders landed on Tanegashima.

lessons.title: Lisbon
lessons.summary: Hills, trams, river light and nearly 3,000 years of history in Portugal's capital.

cards.title: A city on seven hills

deep.x: The "seven hills" idea was popularised in 1620 by the writer Frei Nicolau de Oliveira, who wanted Lisbon to stand comparison with Rome. The usual list is São Jorge, São Vicente, Sant'Ana, Santo André, Chagas, Santa Catarina and São Roque. In reality there are more, and the highest ground, in the Monsanto forest park, is not on the list at all.
An ancient harbour

The site was ideal: hills that were easy to defend, beside a huge sheltered estuary with fresh water and fish. Phoenician traders were probably here by about the 8th century BC. The Romans called the town Olisipo and gave it the title Felicitas Julia. Under Muslim rule it was al-Ushbuna, and in 1147 it was taken by Afonso Henriques.
Small city, big region

x: The municipality covers only about 100 km², smaller than many rural councils
Its population peaked at about 800,000 in 1981, then fell as families moved to the suburbs
The metropolitan area, from Sintra and Cascais across the river to Setúbal, has about 2.9 million people

deep.w: Lisbon was founded by Ulysses
deep.r: A charming legend; the name probably comes from a pre-Roman, possibly Phoenician, word, and its exact origin is unknown

deep.x: Lisbon grew where defensible hills meet a vast sheltered estuary, one of the finest natural harbours in Europe.

cards.text:
Lisbon climbs a set of steep hills on the north bank of the Tagus, just before the river meets the Atlantic. Tradition says there are seven, like Rome.

It is one of Europe's oldest cities and has been Portugal's capital since the 13th century. The city itself is small, but greater Lisbon holds over a quarter of the country's people.

cards.title: Alfama and the Moorish city

deep.x: For about 400 years, from the early 700s to 1147, Lisbon was a Muslim city, part of al-Andalus. Its walled town sat on the castle hill and ran down to the river, roughly where Alfama is now. The name probably comes from al-hamma, "hot springs" or "baths", after warm springs that once rose there.
Layers of history

After the Christian conquest, the Sé, a fortress-like Romanesque cathedral, was built where the main mosque is thought to have stood. Muslims who stayed were moved outside the walls to a district still called Mouraria. The castle on the summit was rebuilt many times; much of what visitors see today is a restoration from the 1940s.
Why it survived 1755

Alfama is often said to have come through the earthquake better because it stands on firmer ground than the soft river silts of the Baixa. Whatever the reason, it is one of the few places where Lisbon's pre-earthquake street plan survives: dead-end alleys (becos), stairways (escadinhas) and little squares (largos).

x: Lisbon fado, sung in small taverns in Alfama and Mouraria, has been UNESCO intangible heritage since 2011
On the night of 12–13 June, the Santo António festival fills the alleys with grilled sardines and pots of basil
Tram 28 squeezes through streets barely wider than the car

deep.x: Mouraria is where the 19th-century singer Maria Severa lived; she is often called the first great fadista.
Alfama is a Moorish street plan that outlived the earthquake and is still lived in after more than a thousand years.

cards.text:
Alfama, below the castle, is Lisbon's oldest quarter. Its name comes from Arabic, and its maze of steep alleys, stairways and tiny squares still follows the shape of the Moorish town.

Much of it survived the 1755 earthquake. Today it is a heartland of Lisbon fado and of the June festivals.

cards.title: Belém

deep.x: In the 1400s this was a beach called Restelo, outside the city, with a small chapel where sailors prayed before leaving. Vasco da Gama is said to have spent the night there before sailing for India in 1497. King Manuel I then built something far grander on the spot.
The Manueline style

Manueline architecture mixes late Gothic structure with carved ropes, anchors, armillary spheres, exotic plants and sea creatures: the imagery of an empire built on ships. Jerónimos was paid for largely by a tax on the spice trade. Vasco da Gama lies in its church, near a tomb honouring the poet Camões.
The tower and the monument

The Belém Tower was a small fortress guarding the river mouth, built on a rock in the water. The shoreline has since crept out towards it, partly through land reclamation. The Padrão dos Descobrimentos, a stone prow over 50 m tall crowded with navigators, is much newer: a temporary version was made for the 1940 Portuguese World Exhibition, and the permanent one in 1960, for the 500th anniversary of Prince Henry's death.
Modern Belém adds the Centro Cultural de Belém (1992), the riverside MAAT museum (2016) and the Belém Palace, the official home of the President.
Pastéis de Belém have been sold beside the monastery since 1837, using a recipe said to come from its monks and still kept secret.
Belém is the age of voyages written in stone, from 16th-century Manueline carving to 20th-century commemoration.

cards.text:
Belém, on the river west of the centre, is where fleets left for Africa, India and Brazil. Its monuments celebrate that age of voyages.

The Jerónimos Monastery and the Belém Tower, both in the ornate Manueline style, have been UNESCO World Heritage since 1983.

cards.title: Port of the world

deep.x: King Manuel I moved the royal palace from the castle down to the river around 1500, a clear sign of where power and money now lay. The new Ribeira Palace stood beside the Casa da Índia, the royal house that controlled the spice trade, and the shipyards where carracks were built.
What passed through
Most spices were not used in Portugal. They were shipped on to Antwerp, then the trading heart of northern Europe, where the Portuguese crown kept a trading house.
A cosmopolitan city
Lisbon grew to perhaps 100,000 people by the mid-1500s, among the largest cities in Europe. Its main shopping street, Rua Nova dos Mercadores, sold goods from every continent.

x: Africans, most of them enslaved, may have made up around a tenth of the population
Italian, Flemish and German merchant families helped finance the voyages
New Christians, Jews forced to convert in 1497, played a big part in trade

deep.x: Little of this city survives: the palace, the Casa da Índia and Rua Nova all vanished in 1755.
In 1515 a live rhinoceros from India arrived in Lisbon as a gift for King Manuel; Albrecht Dürer's famous woodcut was based on a description and sketch of it.
In the 1500s Lisbon was a hinge between Europe and the wider world, and its riverside showed it.

cards.text:
In the 1500s Lisbon was one of the busiest ports in Europe. Pepper, silk and porcelain from Asia, sugar from Brazil and gold from Africa passed along its riverside.

It was a crowded, cosmopolitan city, with merchants from all over Europe and a large African population, many of them enslaved.

cards.title: After 1755: the Baixa

deep.x: The Baixa is best understood on foot. Start at the river in Praça do Comércio, laid out where the royal palace had stood. Its arcaded buildings now hold ministries, cafés and museums, and in the centre stands the bronze horseman of King José I, by the sculptor Machado de Castro, unveiled in 1775.
Up the grid

The triumphal arch of Rua Augusta was planned soon after the earthquake but only finished in 1873. Beyond it, the pedestrian Rua Augusta runs straight to Rossio, with parallel streets named after old trades, such as Rua do Ouro and Rua da Prata. Rossio itself has the wavy black-and-white pavement known as "mar largo" and a column topped by King Pedro IV.
A second fire

On 25 August 1988 a fire destroyed much of the Chiado, the elegant shopping district on the slope above. The architect Álvaro Siza led the rebuilding, keeping the historic façades and modernising what lay behind them. The Santa Justa lift and the roofless Carmo Convent nearby link the Baixa to this upper town.

deep.w: Every Baixa building is untouched 18th-century work
deep.r: Many interiors were later gutted and rebuilt, and some lost their earthquake-resistant timber frames

deep.x: Under Rua da Prata lie Roman galleries, probably foundations of a riverside building; they are usually flooded and open to visitors only a few days a year.
The Baixa is a planned 18th-century city you can read from end to end, from river square to Rossio.

cards.text:
The 1755 earthquake, tsunami and fire destroyed the lower town. It was rebuilt as the Baixa, a grid of straight streets running from the river to Rossio.

Today you can walk the whole plan in about fifteen minutes, from the riverside square, under a triumphal arch, to the old city squares.

cards.title: Trams and lifts

deep.x: Horse-drawn trams on rails, called "americanos" because the idea came from the United States, arrived in 1873. Electric trams followed in 1901. Over the 20th century buses and the Metro took over most routes, and only a handful of tram lines survive.
Why the small trams survive

The classic "remodelado" trams were built in the 1930s and 1940s and rebuilt in the 1990s with new motors and brakes. They are short and narrow, so they can take the tight bends and steep slopes of Alfama and Graça, where modern trams would not fit.
Funiculars and a lift

x: Lavra (1884), Glória (1885) and Bica (1892) are funiculars: two cars joined by a cable, one going up as the other comes down
The Santa Justa lift (1902), a neo-Gothic iron tower, links the Baixa to the Carmo square

deep.x: In September 2025 a crash on the Glória funicular killed 16 people, and the city's funiculars were stopped for safety inspections.

deep.w: The Santa Justa lift was designed by Eiffel
deep.r: It was designed by Raoul Mesnier du Ponsard, an engineer born in Porto to French parents

deep.x: Lisbon's quirky transport is an answer to geography: small trams, cables and lifts for a city of steep hills.

cards.text:
Lisbon's hills made getting around hard, so the city built funiculars, a street lift and a tram network. The small yellow trams, like the famous number 28, still rattle through the old quarters.

Underground runs the Metro, opened in 1959, with four lines and many stations decorated with azulejos.

cards.title: Miradouros and Lisbon light

deep.x: A miradouro is a public terrace on a hilltop or slope, usually with trees, a kiosk and a bench. Most were laid out in the 19th and 20th centuries, as the views came to be treated as something everyone shared. Many sit at the end of a steep climb, so locals often time a visit with a tram or lift ride up.
Where to look
Why the light is special

Lisbon is one of the sunniest capitals in Europe, with about 2,800 hours of sunshine a year. The Tagus estuary, more than 10 km wide in places, acts like a huge mirror, and white limestone pavements and pale façades bounce the light back up. Clean Atlantic air helps too, and painters and photographers have long been drawn to it.

x: Sunset over the river is best from Santa Catarina or the riverside at Cais do Sodré
Many miradouros have kiosks selling drinks and snacks, revived since the 2000s
Morning light from the east is best at Graça and Senhora do Monte

deep.x: The statue at the Santa Catarina viewpoint is Adamastor, the storm giant who, in Camões's epic The Lusiads, guards the Cape of Good Hope.
Lisbon's viewpoints turn a tiring, hilly city into a free open-air gallery of light and roofs.

cards.text:
Lisbon's hills give it dozens of miradouros: public viewpoints with benches, kiosks and views over red roofs to the river.

The city is also famous for its light. Strong sun, reflected off the wide Tagus and pale limestone pavements, gives it a bright, golden glow.

cards.title: Bridges over the Tagus

deep.x: Before 1966 the nearest fixed crossing was far upstream at Vila Franca de Xira, opened in 1951. Commuters from the south bank relied on ferries, the cacilheiros. The new bridge transformed the south bank: Almada, Seixal and Barreiro grew into big suburbs.
The 25 de Abril Bridge

It opened on 6 August 1966 as the Salazar Bridge and was renamed after the 1974 revolution. Its main span was then the longest of any suspension bridge in Europe. It was designed to take trains as well, but the lower rail deck was added only in 1999. On the south bank, the Cristo Rei statue (1959) looks back over the city.

deep.w: It was built by the makers of the Golden Gate
deep.r: It is a separate 1960s design, built by the American Bridge Company, which had worked on San Francisco's other great bridge, the Bay Bridge

deep.x: The Vasco da Gama Bridge
Built for Expo 98, it crosses the widest part of the estuary, from Sacavém to Montijo, for about 12 km. Its piles go deep into soft river mud, and it was designed to resist a very strong earthquake.
A third crossing, between Chelas and Barreiro, is planned together with the new Lisbon airport at Alcochete.
Lisbon's bridges stitched the two banks of the Tagus into one metropolis.

cards.text:
For centuries, crossing the Tagus at Lisbon meant taking a boat. In 1966 a great red suspension bridge opened, today called the 25 de Abril. In 1998 the Vasco da Gama Bridge followed, one of the longest in Europe.

Ferries still cross too, linking Lisbon with Cacilhas, Seixal and Barreiro.

cards.title: Parque das Nações

deep.x: The Expo was planned as the first stage of a new piece of city. The area covered over 300 hectares along the river, and the fair's income and land sales were meant to pay for cleaning it up, building infrastructure and later housing.
Architecture as the attraction

Gare do Oriente, by the Spanish architect Santiago Calatrava, has a platform roof of steel and glass shaped like a forest canopy. Álvaro Siza's Portugal Pavilion is famous for a thin concrete canopy that sags like a sheet of paper between two porticoes. The Oceanário, by the American Peter Chermayeff, is built around one huge central tank holding millions of litres of seawater.
A new neighbourhood

x: Over 20,000 people now live in the area
The large arena built as the Pavilhão Atlântico hosts concerts and the Web Summit
A cable car and riverside gardens run along the water

deep.x: The Vasco da Gama Bridge, Oriente station and the Metro's new red line were all built for the same 1998 deadline.

deep.w: The Expo buildings were knocked down afterwards
deep.r: Most landmarks were kept and reused, as the plan intended from the start

deep.x: Expo 98 used a four-month fair to pay for a permanent new piece of city.

cards.text:
Expo 98 transformed about 5 km of Lisbon's eastern waterfront, an area of oil depots, warehouses and a slaughterhouse.

After the fair closed, the site became Parque das Nações, a new district of homes, offices and gardens with some of Portugal's best-known modern architecture.

cards.title: Lisbon today

deep.x: In 2011 Portugal needed an international bailout, and parts of central Lisbon were half-empty, with crumbling buildings. Within a decade the picture changed. Cheap flights, a 2012 law that freed up rents, tax breaks for new foreign residents, golden visas and online short-term rentals (alojamento local) brought money and people.
Winners and losers

The restoration of old buildings and new jobs in tourism and tech were real gains. The Web Summit, one of the world's largest technology conferences, has been held in Lisbon since 2016. But in some Alfama and Mouraria streets a large share of homes became tourist flats, and long-time residents moved out.

x: New short-term rental licences in the historic centre have been restricted since the late 2010s
Golden visas through property purchase were ended in 2023

deep.x: Looking ahead

Lisbon was European Green Capital in 2020. A new airport is planned at Alcochete, south of the Tagus, to replace the cramped Humberto Delgado airport inside the city, and the Metro is being extended with a circular line.

deep.w: Lisbon is shrinking because people leave the region
deep.r: Most moved within the metropolitan area, whose population has kept growing

deep.x: Lisbon's challenge now is to stay a city for those who live in it, not only a destination for those who visit.

cards.text:
Since the 2010s Lisbon has become one of Europe's most visited cities and a hub for start-ups. Old buildings have been restored and the centre buzzes with visitors.

The boom has a cost: rents and house prices have risen far faster than wages, pushing many residents out of the historic quarters.

quiz.q: Where does the name Alfama probably come from?
quiz.explain: A trace of the Moorish city.

quiz.q: Which two Belém monuments are UNESCO World Heritage?
quiz.explain: Both listed in 1983.

quiz.q: When did the 25 de Abril Bridge open?
quiz.explain: As the Salazar Bridge, renamed after 1974.

quiz.q: Who designed the Santa Justa lift?
quiz.explain: A Porto-born engineer of French parents.

lessons.title: Porto and the North
lessons.summary: The city that named a country and a wine, and the green granite north around it.

cards.title: From Portus Cale to Porto

deep.x: The hill where Porto Cathedral stands, the Morro da Sé, has been lived on since the Iron Age. Under Roman rule, the road from Lisbon to Braga crossed the Douro here, and a port grew on the river. Later the Suevi and Visigoths held the area, and by the 6th century the town had a bishop.
A city of merchants and bishops

In 1120 Countess Teresa gave the town to its bishop, and for centuries bishops and citizens argued over who ran it. Porto's wealth came from trade, fishing and shipbuilding, not from a royal court. By tradition, nobles were not even allowed to stay in the city for more than three days.
Two nicknames

x: **Tripeiros**: in 1415 the city is said to have given all its meat to the fleet sailing to conquer Ceuta, keeping only the tripe. Tripas à moda do Porto is still a local dish
**Invicta**: in 1832–33 Liberal forces under Dom Pedro held Porto through a year-long siege by the absolutist army of his brother Miguel

deep.x: Dom Pedro was so grateful that he left his heart to the city; it is still kept in the Lapa church.
Porto is a city built by merchants rather than kings, and proud of it.

cards.text:
Porto grew on a granite hill above the Douro, near the river's mouth. Its Roman port, Portus Cale, gave its name to Portugal.

A proud merchant city, it is nicknamed "Invicta", the unconquered, and its people are "tripeiros", tripe-eaters, after a story from 1415.

cards.title: The Ribeira

deep.x: For centuries the Ribeira was Porto's working heart. Boats unloaded at the quay, merchants traded under the arcades of Praça da Ribeira, and families lived above their shops in houses only a few metres wide but four or five storeys tall. Tiles and paint protected the façades from the damp. By the 1970s much of the quarter was run-down and overcrowded, and its restoration since the 1980s helped win UNESCO status.

items: Sé and Clérigos on the hilltop

deep.x: Treasures nearby

x: The **Palácio da Bolsa**, the 19th-century stock exchange, has a lavish "Arab Room" inspired by the Alhambra
**São Francisco church** looks plain outside but is covered inside with gilded carved wood (talha dourada)
The **Clérigos Tower**, about 75 m tall, by the Italian-born architect Nicolau Nasoni, was finished in 1763

deep.x: Living with the river

The Douro can rise many metres in winter floods. Plaques on Ribeira walls mark the highest levels; the flood of 1909 was among the worst. Since big dams were built upstream, floods are less frequent, but not gone.
The UNESCO site also includes the Serra do Pilar monastery on the Gaia side, from where the classic view of the Ribeira is taken.
The Ribeira is Porto's postcard: a vertical city of narrow houses, tied to the river that made it rich.

cards.text:
The Ribeira is Porto's old riverside quarter: tall, narrow houses in bright colours stacked up the slope above the Douro quay.

Together with the old centre and the Dom Luís I Bridge, it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1996.

cards.title: Porto's bridges

deep.x: Before the 19th century the Douro at Porto was crossed by boat and, from 1806, by a bridge of boats. In 1809, during the French invasion, it gave way under crowds fleeing the troops, and many hundreds of people drowned.
The age of iron

When the railway from Lisbon reached the Douro, engineers had to span a deep gorge. Eiffel's company won with the Maria Pia Bridge (1877), a single wrought-iron arch of 160 m, then the longest of its kind in the world. Its engineer, Théophile Seyrig, later left Eiffel and designed the Dom Luís I Bridge (1886), whose arch spans 172 m.

deep.w: Eiffel designed the Dom Luís I Bridge
deep.r: It was designed by Théophile Seyrig, Eiffel's former partner; Eiffel's company built the Maria Pia upstream

deep.x: The age of concrete

The engineer Edgar Cardoso designed the Arrábida Bridge (1963), whose concrete arch of 270 m was then the longest in the world, and the São João railway bridge (1991), which replaced the Maria Pia. The Freixo (1995) and Infante D. Henrique (2003) bridges complete the six.
Visitors can now walk over the top of the Arrábida arch on guided climbs.
Porto's bridges are a museum of engineering, from 19th-century iron to 20th-century concrete.

cards.text:
Six bridges cross the Douro between Porto and Gaia. The iron Maria Pia railway bridge (1877) was built by Gustave Eiffel's company.

The Dom Luís I Bridge (1886) has two decks: the upper one now carries the Metro, the lower one cars and walkers beside the Ribeira.

cards.title: Port wine

deep.x: Yeast turns grape sugar into alcohol. If winemakers add a clear grape spirit (aguardente) of about 77% alcohol when only part of the sugar has fermented, the yeast stops working and the rest of the sugar stays in the wine. The result is sweet, strong and keeps well.

x: About 4 parts fermenting grape juice
+ 1 part grape spirit at 77%
Sweet wine of about 19–22% alcohol

deep.x: Why the British loved it

Wars with France in the late 1600s cut England off from French wine. The Methuen Treaty of 1703 lowered duties on Portuguese wine, and British merchants set up firms in Porto and Gaia. Names such as Taylor's, Croft, Graham's and Sandeman still show that history.
Styles

Ruby ports age briefly and keep a deep red colour and fresh fruit. Tawny ports age for years in small wooden casks, slowly turning amber and nutty. Vintage port comes from a single outstanding year, ages mostly in the bottle and can last for decades. Today the Douro and Port Wine Institute controls quality and labels.
Until 1986, port had to be aged and shipped from the lodges of Vila Nova de Gaia; only then could Douro farms export directly.
Port is wine with its fermentation deliberately stopped, a trick that made it sweet, strong and able to travel.

cards.text:
Port is a fortified wine from the Douro. Adding grape spirit part-way through fermentation stops the yeast, leaving natural sweetness and about 20% alcohol.

For centuries the wine was shipped down the river and aged in the lodges of Vila Nova de Gaia, opposite Porto, before export.

cards.title: The Douro valley

deep.x: The wine valley stretches for about 100 km towards the Spanish border. Mountains to the west, especially the Serra do Marão, block much of the Atlantic rain, so the upper valley has hot, dry summers, often above 40 °C, and cold winters. Vines thrive in the poor, stony schist, which splits into layers that roots can follow deep down to find water.
Built by hand

The slopes are so steep that almost everything was done by hand. Workers broke the schist and built dry-stone walls to make narrow terraces (socalcos). Later terraces were cut by machine into wider earth banks (patamares), and some newer vineyards run straight up and down the slope.
Crisis and recovery

From the 1860s phylloxera, a tiny insect from America that attacks vine roots, killed most of the vines. Many terraces were abandoned and can still be seen as overgrown "mortórios". Vines were replanted on American rootstocks, which resist the pest.

x: Baixo Corgo is the wettest sub-region, Cima Corgo around Pinhão the heart of port, and Douro Superior the driest
The September harvest is still largely done by hand, and some quintas still tread grapes by foot in stone tanks called lagares

deep.x: The railway station at Pinhão is decorated with azulejo panels showing scenes of Douro life and the harvest.
The Douro is a landscape built by people, stone by stone, to grow wine where little else would grow.

cards.text:
Upstream from Porto, the Douro cuts through steep schist hills that people have carved into terraces of vines over centuries.

The Alto Douro Wine Region, one of the oldest demarcated wine regions in the world, has been a UNESCO cultural landscape since 2001.

cards.title: Rabelo boats

deep.x: Before the railway, the Douro was the only practical road out of the wine valley. After the wine had rested through the winter, barrels called pipes, of about 550 litres each, were loaded onto rabelos at riverside quays and carried downstream to the lodges in Gaia.
A dangerous river

The Douro was then fast and full of rapids and rocks. A crew of a handful of men steered with the long oar from a raised platform at the stern, using the current to go down. Coming back, they sailed with the sea breeze and were towed from the bank. Many boats and lives were lost.
The worst obstacle was the Cachão da Valeira gorge, which blocked boats completely until rocks were blasted away in the 1780s and 1790s, opening the upper Douro.
The end of an era
Five dams on the Portuguese Douro now have locks; the one at Carrapatelo lifts boats about 35 m, one of the highest in Europe. Today cruise boats, not rabelos, carry most people up the valley.
Since the 1980s the port houses have raced their rabelos at the mouth of the Douro on 24 June, São João's day.
The rabelo was the Douro's lorry, built for a wild river that dams have since tamed.

cards.text:
For centuries, port wine travelled from the Douro farms to Gaia in rabelos: flat-bottomed wooden boats with a square sail and a long steering oar.

Railways, roads and dams ended the trade, but rabelos still float by the Gaia lodges and race on São João's day.

cards.title: Braga and Guimarães

deep.x: Braga began as Bracara Augusta, founded around 16 BC under Emperor Augustus, and later became the capital of the Roman province of Gallaecia. In the 5th and 6th centuries it was the capital of the Suevi kingdom. Its archbishops long claimed to be "primate of the Spains", the senior churchmen of all Iberia, a title disputed with Toledo.
Bom Jesus do Monte

Above Braga, a zigzag Baroque stairway climbs a wooded hill to a church. Its chapels and fountains represent the Stations of the Cross, the five senses and the three virtues, and pilgrims traditionally climb it, some on their knees. Beside it runs a funicular from 1882 that is powered by water.
Guimarães

Guimarães grew around a 10th-century monastery founded by Countess Mumadona Dias and a castle built to protect it. Its granite streets, squares and balconied houses were carefully restored from the 1980s, earning UNESCO listing in 2001. It was a European Capital of Culture in 2012, and today its university and young population keep the old centre lively.
The Bom Jesus funicular is the oldest in the world still working by water counterweight, carrying people up the hill since 1882.
Braga and Guimarães hold the deep roots of the north: Roman, religious and royal.

cards.text:
Two old cities of the Minho sit about 25 km apart. Braga, founded by the Romans, has been a religious capital for over 1,500 years and is crowded with churches.

Guimarães, linked to Portugal's first king, has a beautifully kept medieval centre listed by UNESCO.

cards.title: Granite and green

deep.x: Much of northern Portugal sits on granite and schist formed around 300 million years ago, when ancient continents collided to build the supercontinent Pangaea. Molten rock cooled slowly deep underground into granite, and erosion has since brought it to the surface as rounded hills and huge boulders.
A granite culture

Because granite was everywhere, northern builders used it for almost everything: house walls, steps, window frames, wayside crosses, wine presses, granaries and posts for vines. In Porto, granite door and window frames contrast with façades covered in coloured azulejos.
Why so green

Wet winds from the Atlantic rise over the coastal mountains and drop their rain. The Peneda-Gerês mountains receive around 3,000 mm in a year, among the highest totals in Europe, while parts of the Alentejo get less than a fifth of that.

x: Land is split into many small plots, a legacy of inheritance shared among children
The Minho has long been one of the most densely settled rural areas of Portugal
Rivers rise fast after storms and have powered mills for centuries

deep.x: Granite contains traces of uranium, so radon gas can build up in old stone houses; ventilating ground floors and cellars keeps levels down.
The north is a land of granite and rain: hard stone underfoot and green growth all around.

cards.text:
The north-west of Portugal is built of granite and soaked by Atlantic rain. Walls, houses, churches and even vine posts are made of it.

Mild, wet weather keeps the Minho green all year, with small fields, woods and fast rivers flowing down from the mountains.

cards.title: The industrious North

deep.x: Industry in the North grew from water and people. Fast rivers like the Ave powered 19th-century textile mills, and the crowded countryside supplied workers who often kept a small farm on the side. Small and medium-sized family firms, rather than giant factories, became the norm.
Shock and recovery

When China joined the World Trade Organization in 2001 and global textile quotas ended in 2005, many northern factories closed and unemployment rose in the Ave valley. The survivors changed strategy: technical fabrics, small and fast orders for European fashion brands, and their own labels. Being two or three days by lorry from Paris or Madrid became an advantage over factories on the other side of the world.
Products the world knows

x: Portuguese shoes fetch some of the highest average export prices in the world, behind Italy
Portugal is the world's largest cork producer, and the biggest cork company, Amorim, is based near Santa Maria da Feira
Guimarães, Barcelos and Famalicão are centres for textiles and home linens

deep.w: Portugal's economy is just tourism
deep.r: Manufacturing, much of it in the North, still provides a large share of the country's exports

deep.x: The North's family factories survived globalisation by competing on quality, speed and design rather than cheapness.

cards.text:
The North is Portugal's manufacturing heartland. Thousands of family firms make textiles, clothing, shoes, furniture and cork products, much of it for export.

After hard years of competition from Asia, many moved upmarket, selling design, speed and quality rather than low prices.

cards.title: Porto today

deep.x: Porto was a European Capital of Culture in 2001, which launched projects that changed the city: the Casa da Música concert hall by the Dutch architect Rem Koolhaas, opened in 2005, and the Metro do Porto, whose first line opened in 2002.
The Porto school

The city's architecture school, shaped for decades by Fernando Távora and then Siza, became known for buildings that are simple, often white, carefully fitted to their site and made of local materials. Siza's tidal swimming pools at Leça da Palmeira, set into the rocks by the sea, are a famous early work from 1966. Students and visitors now come to Porto just to see these buildings.
Daily life

x: The Metro is mostly light rail and runs across the top deck of the Dom Luís I Bridge
The francesinha, a sandwich of meats under melted cheese and a beer-and-tomato sauce, is the local comfort food
Like Lisbon, Porto faces rising rents as tourist flats spread through the historic centre

deep.w: Livraria Lello inspired Hogwarts in Harry Potter
deep.r: J.K. Rowling, who lived in Porto in the early 1990s, has said she never visited the bookshop

deep.x: Porto has joined its granite old town and bold new buildings into one confident identity.

cards.text:
Porto has reinvented itself since the 2000s, with landmark architecture, a light-rail Metro, a booming tourist trade and lively universities.

It is also Portugal's architecture capital: Álvaro Siza and Eduardo Souto de Moura, both Pritzker Prize winners, come from the Porto school.

quiz.q: Who designed the Dom Luís I Bridge?
quiz.explain: Eiffel's former partner; Eiffel's firm built the Maria Pia.

quiz.q: How does port wine keep its sweetness?
quiz.explain: The yeast stops before all the sugar is used.

quiz.q: What were rabelo boats used for?
options: Carrying port wine down the Douro
quiz.explain: Pipes of wine went from the farms to Gaia.

quiz.q: Why is Porto nicknamed "Invicta"?
options: It held out through the 1832–33 siege
quiz.explain: Liberal forces resisted Miguel's army.

lessons.title: Azores and Madeira
lessons.summary: Volcanic islands in the Atlantic: how they formed, who settled them and how they live today.

cards.title: Born from the ocean floor

deep.x: At the Mid-Atlantic Ridge the sea floor is pulling apart by roughly 2 cm a year, and molten rock wells up to fill the gap. Near the Azores this happens across an unusually broad zone, the Azores plateau, probably because a plume of hot mantle also rises beneath it. The extra melt built a cluster of volcanoes tall enough to break the surface.
Hotspot islands

Madeira formed differently. It sits over a hotspot, a long-lived column of hot mantle, while the African plate creeps slowly over it. Each volcano is carried away from the source and goes quiet, and a new one grows above the hotspot. That is why Porto Santo, to the north-east, is much older and more worn down than Madeira.
Youngest and oldest

x: **Santa Maria**, the oldest Azorean island, is the only one with marine fossils and pale sandy beaches
**Pico**, the youngest, is a near-perfect cone reaching 2,351 m, the highest point in Portugal
Porto Santo's long golden beach is made of crushed shells and old reef, not volcanic rock

deep.x: Because the islands are so young, their soils are thin on the newest lava and rich on older ash, and their coasts are mostly steep cliffs.

deep.w: The Azores are the peaks of sunken Atlantis
deep.r: They are young volcanoes built up from the sea floor; Atlantis is a legend told by Plato

deep.x: Island Portugal was made by fire from below: the Azores by plates pulling apart, Madeira by a hotspot.

cards.text:
Both archipelagos are the tops of huge volcanoes that rise thousands of metres from the Atlantic floor.
