The Azores sit where three tectonic plates meet, near the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. Madeira lies in the middle of the African plate, above a hotspot of hot, rising mantle rock.

cards.title: Volcanoes still awake

deep.x: Since the Portuguese arrived, the Azores have seen many eruptions, on land and offshore, and hundreds of felt earthquakes. Madeira, by contrast, has had no eruption in historical times.
Capelinhos

In September 1957 a volcano began erupting from the sea just off the western tip of Faial. For about 13 months it threw out ash, steam and lava, building a new peninsula of about 2.4 km² and burying nearby villages and the lighthouse in ash. No one died, but farms and homes were ruined.

In 1958 the US Congress passed the Azorean Refugee Act, backed by Senator John F. Kennedy, which offered special visas to families hit by the eruption and opened the way for a large wave of emigration.
Earthquakes and landslides

In 1522 an earthquake set off a landslide that buried Vila Franca do Campo, then the main town of São Miguel, killing thousands. On 1 January 1980 an earthquake of about magnitude 7 struck Terceira, São Jorge and Graciosa, killing about 60 people and badly damaging Angra do Heroísmo, which was rebuilt and listed by UNESCO in 1983.
Living with it
The Capelinhos visitor centre is built underground, inside the ash, beside the half-buried old lighthouse.
The Azores' volcanoes give them fertile soils and clean energy, and occasionally take lives and homes.

cards.text:
The Azores are still geologically active. Earthquakes are frequent, and several volcanoes have erupted since settlement, both on land and under the sea.

The 1957–58 Capelinhos eruption on Faial added new land to the island and led thousands of islanders to emigrate to the United States.

cards.title: Empty islands

deep.x: Madeira was explored by João Gonçalves Zarco and Tristão Vaz Teixeira around 1419–20, sent by Prince Henry. Its name means "wood", after the dense forest. Settlers arrived from about 1425, and the islands were split into captaincies, each run by a captain on behalf of the crown.
Bartolomeu Perestrelo's daughter Filipa later married Christopher Columbus, who lived for a time on Porto Santo and in Madeira.
Clearing the land

Chroniclers tell that settlers set fire to Madeira's forest and it burned for seven years. That is surely exaggerated, but huge areas were cleared. Rabbits released on Porto Santo multiplied so fast that they ruined early crops. In the Azores, sheep, goats and pigs were often left on islands before settlers arrived, so there would be food waiting.
Who came

Most settlers came from the Algarve, Alentejo and Minho. On Faial and Pico, Flemish families arrived under Josse van Huerter, whose name is said to survive in the town of Horta. Enslaved Africans were also brought, especially to Madeira's sugar plantations.
Lake sediments studied in 2021 hinted that people may have visited the Azores centuries before the Portuguese, perhaps Norse sailors, but the idea is still debated.
The islands were empty when found, so their people, crops and even animals all came with 15th-century settlement.

cards.text:
Unlike the Canary Islands, Madeira and the Azores had no native people when Portuguese sailors arrived in the early 1400s.

Settlers came from mainland Portugal and, on some Azorean islands, from Flanders. They cleared forest, brought animals and crops, and built new societies from scratch.

cards.title: Sugar, oranges and tea

deep.x: Madeira's white gold

Sugar cane thrived on Madeira's warm south side. By around 1500 Madeira was the leading sugar producer of the Atlantic world, worked largely by enslaved people from Africa and the Canaries, and its mills and water channels became a model later copied in São Tomé and Brazil. Brazil's larger, cheaper sugar soon undercut it, and Madeira turned to wine.
The Azores' crops

Early settlers grew wheat for Portugal's forts in North Africa and woad (pastel), a plant whose blue dye sold well in Flanders. Angra, on Terceira, became a vital stop for fleets returning from India and Brazil. In the 1800s São Miguel shipped huge numbers of oranges, mostly to Britain, until disease and competition ended the trade from the 1860s.
Growers then tried new crops. Pineapples were raised in glasshouses, and tea was planted with the help of experts brought from Macau in 1878.
Today

x: Cows are said to outnumber people in the Azores, and cheeses like São Jorge are famous
Madeira grows bananas on terraces, mostly sold to mainland Portugal
Tourism is now the biggest earner in Madeira and growing fast in the Azores

deep.x: Azorean pineapple plants are "smoked" inside glasshouses with burning green plant matter, a traditional trick that makes them flower at the same time.
The islands survived by switching crops whenever markets changed, from sugar and dye to oranges, milk and visitors.

cards.text:
The islands' economies have changed again and again. Madeira had a sugar boom in the late 1400s, then turned to wine. The Azores grew wheat and dye plants, then exported oranges to Britain.

Today dairy farming dominates the Azores, while tourism leads in Madeira.

cards.title: An Atlantic climate

deep.x: The sea changes temperature slowly, so islands far from land rarely get very hot or very cold. In Funchal, winter afternoons are often around 19–20 °C and summer days rarely pass 30 °C. Frost happens only on the highest peaks, where snow falls now and then in winter.
The Azores High

The Azores lie near a zone of high pressure over the subtropical Atlantic, the Azores High. In summer it usually grows and shelters the islands, giving long settled spells. In winter it often shifts south, and Atlantic depressions sweep through with rain and gales. The Azores therefore get much less sunshine than Madeira, and hydrangeas thrive in the damp.
Storms and floods

x: In October 2019 Hurricane Lorenzo passed close to Flores and Corvo and wrecked much of the port at Lajes das Flores
In February 2010 flash floods and mudslides in Madeira killed more than 40 people, mostly around Funchal
On steep islands, heavy rain turns into a torrent within minutes

deep.x: Madeira now builds channels and barriers in its ravines to slow these floods.
The Azores are not tropical: the sea around them is usually about 16 °C in late winter and around 23 °C at the end of summer.
The ocean is the islands' thermostat: mild all year, but open to storms from every side.

cards.text:
The ocean keeps both archipelagos mild all year. Madeira is subtropical, with warm winters on its sunny south coast. The Azores are cooler, wetter and windier, with changeable skies.

The mountains create big contrasts: wet, cloudy north slopes and drier south coasts.

cards.title: Laurel forest survivors

deep.x: Laurisilva is a humid evergreen forest found in Macaronesia, the island groups of the Azores, Madeira and the Canaries. Each archipelago has its own endemic species, because plants and animals that arrived from the mainland evolved in isolation for millions of years.
The Azores' lost forest

When settlers arrived, laurel and juniper forest covered much of the Azores. Today native forest survives mainly on steep slopes, high ridges and in protected areas. Much of the land is pasture, or plantations of Japanese cedar (cryptomeria), a fast-growing timber tree introduced in the 1800s.
Invaders

x: Kahili ginger (conteira), a showy Himalayan plant, smothers the forest floor and stream banks
Australian cheesewood (incenso) has spread across lowland woods
Rangers and volunteers clear invaders and replant native species

deep.x: The priolo

The Azores bullfinch, or priolo, lives only in the native forest around Pico da Vara in eastern São Miguel. In the 1990s just a few hundred birds were thought to survive, making it one of Europe's rarest birds. Removing invaders and replanting the native plants whose seeds and buds it eats helped numbers rise to around a thousand, and its threat status has been lowered.

deep.w: Laurel forest is just a wood of bay trees
deep.r: It is a whole ecosystem of several laurel-family trees with heathers, hollies, ferns, mosses and lichens

deep.x: Laurisilva is a living relic, and on most islands it survives only where people have chosen to protect it.

cards.text:
Madeira's laurel forest is a famous survivor, but laurisilva once covered much of the Azores too. There, most was cut down for fields and pasture, and invasive plants now threaten the rest.

Protecting these forests also protects rare island birds such as the priolo of São Miguel.

cards.title: From whaling to whale-watching

deep.x: Whaling came to the Azores with American ships from New England, which stopped in the islands for water, food and crew. Many young Azoreans signed on, and some settled in New Bedford, Massachusetts. In the 1800s islanders started their own shore-based whaling.
How it worked

Lookouts in stone huts on the cliffs, the vigias, scanned the sea. When they saw a spout, they fired a rocket, and men ran from fields and homes to the boats. The canoas were light, about 11 m long, and rowed or sailed by a crew of seven. The harpooner struck by hand, and a wounded whale could drag the boat for hours. Oil was then extracted at shore factories.
The end of the hunt
Sea giants today

x: Sperm whales live around the islands all year
Blue, fin and sei whales pass through in spring on migration
Common, bottlenose and Risso's dolphins are seen on most trips

deep.x: The whalers' museum at Lajes do Pico keeps the boats, tools and stories of the hunt.
In Moby-Dick (1851), Herman Melville noted that many whaling crews were filled out with hardy Azorean islanders.
The Azores turned a hunting tradition into a watching one, using the same lookouts and knowledge of the sea.

cards.text:
For about a century, Azorean men hunted sperm whales from small open boats with hand-thrown harpoons. The last one was killed in 1987.

Two years later the first whale-watching company started on Pico. Today whale-watching is a major part of the islands' tourism.

cards.title: How autonomy works

deep.x: Autonomy was a response to geography and history. The islands are far from Lisbon, and after the 1974 revolution independence movements briefly appeared in both, notably the FLA in the Azores and FLAMA in Madeira. The 1976 Constitution answered with self-government inside the Portuguese state.
Money and taxes

The regions keep most of the taxes raised on the islands and also receive transfers from the state budget. They may lower some taxes, which is why VAT rates are lower than on the mainland. Madeira also has a low-tax International Business Centre, whose rules have been examined by the European Commission.
Outermost regions
The EU recognises nine outermost regions: the Azores, Madeira, the Canary Islands and six French territories. EU treaties allow special measures for them, such as support for transport and farming.
Politics
Madeira was led for 37 years, from 1978 to 2015, by Alberto João Jardim of the PSD. The Azores were governed by the PS from 1996 to 2020, and since then by a PSD-led coalition.
Lajes air base on Terceira, used by Allied forces since 1943, is still shared by the Portuguese and US air forces.
Autonomy lets the islands govern most daily matters themselves while remaining fully part of Portugal and the EU.

cards.text:
Since 1976 the Azores and Madeira have been autonomous regions, with their own elected parliaments and governments that run most local affairs.

They are also "outermost regions" of the European Union, which allows special support and rules because of their distance and small island economies.

cards.title: Madeira wine

deep.x: In the 1600s and 1700s, ships bound for India and the Americas called at Funchal and took casks of wine aboard. Merchants noticed that wine which had crossed the tropics and come back, called vinho da roda ("round-trip wine"), tasted better. Producers then found ways to copy the effect at home.
How it is made

Like port, Madeira is fortified with grape spirit, added early for sweet styles and late for dry ones. Then comes the warming. Because the wine has already been heated and exposed to air, an opened bottle keeps for months, and some bottles from the 1700s and 1800s are still drinkable.

x: **Sercial**: the driest, sharp and fresh
**Verdelho**: medium-dry
**Boal** (Bual): medium-rich
**Malvasia** (Malmsey): the richest and sweetest
**Tinta Negra**, a red grape, is the workhorse of most everyday blends

deep.x: Famous fans

Madeira was a favourite wine in colonial America, and it is often said that it was used to toast the US Declaration of Independence in 1776. Shakespeare mentions Malmsey, and an old story says the Duke of Clarence was drowned in a barrel of it in 1478.

deep.w: Madeira is just a cooking wine
deep.r: Cheap cooking Madeira exists, but the best are among the longest-lived fine wines in the world

deep.x: Madeira is the wine that thrives on the heat and air that ruin other wines.

cards.text:
Madeira wine is fortified like port, but then deliberately warmed for months or years. This "cooking" gives it nutty, caramel flavours and makes it almost indestructible.

Four classic grapes give four styles, from dry Sercial to rich, sweet Malvasia, also called Malmsey.

cards.title: Islands of emigrants

deep.x: Small islands with large families and little land could not support everyone. Waves of emigration followed hardship: eruptions, earthquakes, crop failures and lack of work. Most Portuguese Americans, about 1.4 million people, have Azorean roots. Money sent home by emigrants paid for houses, churches and festas across the islands.
Communities abroad

In the US, cities such as Fall River and New Bedford in Massachusetts, and farming towns in California's Central Valley, have large Azorean communities with their own Holy Spirit festas. Madeirans built a big community in Venezuela; since that country's economic crisis in the 2010s, many have returned to Madeira.
New arrivals

x: Low-cost flights to Ponta Delgada began after air links were opened up in 2015, and Azores tourism grew fast
Madeira's airport, named after Cristiano Ronaldo in 2017, has a runway extended over the sea on tall concrete pillars
Remote workers have settled in places like Ponta do Sol, Madeira, which opened a "Digital Nomad Village" in 2021

deep.x: Funchal's New Year fireworks were recognised by Guinness World Records in 2006 as the largest fireworks display in the world.
The islands' story is one of leaving and returning: emigrants carried their culture abroad, and now the world comes to them.

cards.text:
For centuries, island life meant emigration. Azoreans went to Brazil, then to New England, California and Canada. Madeirans went to Venezuela, South Africa, Brazil and the UK.

Emigrant communities keep close ties with home, while tourism, cheaper flights and remote work now bring new people to the islands.

quiz.q: What formed Madeira?
options: A hotspot under the African plate
A piece of Africa that broke off
quiz.explain: The plate slides slowly over a hot column of mantle.

quiz.q: Which eruption of 1957–58 led to emigration to the USA?
quiz.explain: The US passed the Azorean Refugee Act in 1958.

quiz.q: When was the last sperm whale hunted in the Azores?
quiz.explain: Whale-watching began two years later.

quiz.q: What makes Madeira wine distinctive?
options: It is aged under the sea
quiz.explain: By estufagem or canteiro warming.

lessons.title: The Portuguese language
lessons.summary: From the Latin of Gallaecia to a global language of about 260 million speakers.

cards.title: From Latin to Portuguese

deep.x: The Romans landed in Iberia in 218 BC, during their war with Carthage, and needed about two centuries to conquer the west. The Lusitanians, led by Viriathus, resisted fiercely until he was murdered in 139 BC. Soldiers, traders and settlers brought not the polished Latin of Cicero but the everyday spoken Latin, often called Vulgar Latin.
Regular sound changes
Portuguese is easy to recognise by a few changes that happened again and again:

x: An l between vowels disappeared: dolorem became dor, salire became sair
An n between vowels vanished, often leaving a nasal vowel: luna became lua, manum became mão
Pl-, cl- and fl- at the start of a word turned into ch-: plenum became cheio, flamma became chama
The group -ct- became -it-: noctem became noite, lactem became leite
Latin pluvia
pl- becomes ch-
Portuguese chuva (rain)

deep.x: Germanic traces

After Rome fell, the Germanic Suebi and then the Visigoths ruled the north-west. They soon adopted Latin but left a few dozen words, many of them military, such as guerra (war), guardar (to guard) and roubar (to rob), plus the colour branco (white).

deep.w: Portuguese is a kind of "broken Spanish"
deep.r: Portuguese and Spanish are sister languages that grew separately from spoken Latin

deep.x: Portuguese is Latin that kept changing, in regular steps, for two thousand years.

cards.text:
Portuguese is a Romance language: it grew out of the everyday Latin spoken in the Roman west of Iberia.

Over many centuries that Latin changed sound by sound until it became a new language. Most Portuguese words still go back to Latin, even when they look very different today.

cards.title: Galician-Portuguese

deep.x: The language took shape between the 9th and 12th centuries in the old Kingdom of Galicia, which reached south to the Douro. Formal documents were still written in Latin, but scribes let local words slip in, and by around 1200 whole texts appeared in the spoken language. Besides Afonso II's will, an early example is the Notícia de Torto, a list of grievances from the same years.
Why they split

x: Portugal's centre moved south to Coimbra and then Lisbon, where the language mixed with the Romance speech of the reconquered south
Galicia was ruled from Castile, so Castilian became the language of power and writing there
Portuguese gained its own court, chancery, university and, later, printing presses

deep.x: Close cousins today

Galician is co-official with Spanish in Galicia, a region of about 2.7 million people. A farmer from the Minho and one from Ourense can usually chat with little effort, and many Galicians watch Portuguese television. Spelling hides some of the closeness: Galician writes ñ and ll where Portuguese writes nh and lh.
Some Galicians, known as reintegrationists, argue that Galician should use Portuguese spelling, and a few associations already write it that way.
Portuguese and Galician began as one language; borders and politics, not distance, pulled them apart.

cards.text:
In the Middle Ages, people on both banks of the Minho spoke one language, now called Galician-Portuguese.

When Portugal became an independent kingdom and expanded south, its speech drifted away from that of Galicia, which came under Castile. Galician and Portuguese are still very close relatives.

cards.title: Words from Arabic

deep.x: The Moors held Lisbon until 1147 and the Algarve until 1249. Christians, Muslims and Jews lived side by side, and many Christians under Muslim rule spoke a Romance dialect full of Arabic terms. As the Portuguese kingdom moved south, it took over farms, irrigation channels, markets and workshops, together with the words for them.
The telltale al-
Arabic al means "the". Portuguese usually borrowed nouns with the article attached, which is why so many Arabic loans start with al- or a-.
Names on the map

x: Alcântara: al-qantara, "the bridge"
Albufeira: al-buhayra, "the lagoon"
Alcácer do Sal: al-qasr, "the castle"
Fátima: an Arabic woman's name, borne by the Prophet's daughter

deep.x: Most of these names cluster south of the Tagus, where Muslim rule lasted longest. In the Minho and Trás-os-Montes they are much rarer.
Oxalá, "let's hope so", probably comes from the Arabic phrase "law sha' Allah", "if God wills"; Spanish has the same word, ojalá.

deep.w: Arabic left only a handful of words
deep.r: Estimates run to several hundred everyday words, and many more counting place names

deep.x: Arabic gave Portuguese a whole layer of everyday words, many still recognisable by the al- at the start.

cards.text:
From 711, much of Iberia was ruled by Muslim states; in what is now southern Portugal, until 1249.

Arabic was the language of learning, farming and trade, and Portuguese absorbed several hundred of its words, from the kitchen to the building site, plus place names all over the south.

cards.title: The troubadours

items: Cantigas de amigo: a girl's voice
Cantigas de amor: a man's lament

deep.x: The fashion began with the troubadours of southern France, whose songs travelled along the pilgrim road to Santiago de Compostela. Poets in north-west Iberia adapted it, and Galician-Portuguese became so prestigious that Castilians wrote poetry in it too. Alfonso X of Castile composed over 400 songs to the Virgin Mary, the Cantigas de Santa Maria, in Galician-Portuguese, even though he wrote his laws in Castilian.
Three kinds of song

items.b: a girl longs for her love
a man pines for a lady

deep.x: The cantigas de amigo are the most original. Though written by men, they speak in a young woman's voice, often by the sea, at a spring or under a hazel tree, waiting for her "amigo". Their refrains and repeated lines suggest roots in older folk songs.
A poet king
King Dinis, who reigned from 1279 to 1325, left about 137 cantigas, more than almost any poet of his time; Alfonso X was his grandfather.

x: Martin Codax, a jogral from Vigo, left seven songs about the sea, six of them with their music, a rare survival
The songs reach us through three main songbooks: the Cancioneiro da Ajuda in Lisbon and two later Italian copies, now in the Vatican Library and Portugal's National Library

deep.x: The insult songs can be startlingly crude: poets mocked cowardly knights, stingy patrons and each other in terms that still make readers blush.
For about 150 years, Galician-Portuguese was the language Iberian poets used to sing about love.

cards.text:
In the 13th and 14th centuries, Galician-Portuguese was the fashionable language of lyric poetry across Christian Iberia.

Kings, nobles and wandering jograis composed songs of love, longing and mockery. About 1,700 of these cantigas survive, copied into a handful of medieval songbooks.

cards.title: Camões and the Lusiads

deep.x: Camões was born around 1524, probably in Lisbon, and lived a restless life. He lost an eye fighting in North Africa, was jailed after a street brawl in Lisbon, and sailed for India in 1553. He spent about 17 years in the East, in Goa and possibly Macau, before returning home poor.
The poem

The epic follows Gama's fleet from Lisbon to Calicut while the gods of Olympus argue over the sailors: Venus protects them and Bacchus plots against them. On the way, characters tell Portuguese history, from Viriathus to Aljubarrota. It opens with "As armas e os barões assinalados", "arms and the famous heroes", an echo of Virgil's Aeneid.
The poem is not pure praise. As the fleet leaves Belém, the Old Man of Restelo condemns the greed and vanity that drive the empire.
Fixing the language

Portuguese grammar was being written down at the same time: Fernão de Oliveira published the first grammar in 1536 and João de Barros another in 1540. Camões's vocabulary and style then served as a model for writers for centuries.
According to tradition, Camões survived a shipwreck at the mouth of the Mekong by swimming ashore with his manuscript held above the water.
Camões turned a sea voyage into the founding poem of the Portuguese language.

cards.text:
Luís Vaz de Camões gave Portuguese its great epic. Os Lusíadas, printed in 1572, retells Vasco da Gama's voyage to India as the story of a whole people.

Its success helped fix Portuguese as a literary language, which is still often called "the language of Camões".

cards.title: Across the oceans

deep.x: Portuguese spread in two different ways. In Brazil, and later in Angola and Mozambique, it became the language of settlers, the state, the Church and schools. In much of Asia it spread as a contact language: merchants, interpreters and local traders used a simplified Portuguese with each other, even when no Portuguese were present. Dutch and English traders arriving in the 1600s often had to learn it to do business.
Creoles
Where people of many origins mixed, new languages formed, with mostly Portuguese words but a grammar of their own.
Papiamento, spoken in Aruba, Curaçao and Bonaire, also has a strong Portuguese element, though linguists debate how it began.
Words that travelled

x: Swahili meza (table), from mesa
Hindi and Bengali chabi (key), from chave, and Konkani and Marathi pav (bread roll), from pão
Japanese kappa (raincoat), from capa
English marmalade, from marmelada, quince paste, and cobra, from cobra de capelo

deep.w: Creoles are just broken Portuguese
deep.r: They are full languages with their own grammar; Kriolu alone is the mother tongue of about a million people

deep.x: Portuguese travelled first as a tool of trade, and it left words and whole new languages wherever ships called.

cards.text:
From the 1400s, Portuguese sailors, traders and missionaries carried their language along the coasts of Africa, Asia and South America.

For about two centuries it served as a common trading language in many ports. It left behind new creole languages and a trail of borrowed words.

cards.title: About 260 million speakers

deep.x: Counting speakers is never exact. Censuses ask different questions, and in Africa many people speak Portuguese as a second or third language alongside local ones. The figure of about 260 million, used by the Instituto Camões among others, includes both native speakers and fluent second-language speakers.
Where they live

x: Portugal, ~10.5 million speakers
÷ ~260 million in total
≈ 4% of all speakers

deep.x: Growing in Africa

Angola and Mozambique have young, fast-growing populations, and Portuguese is spreading as the language of cities, schools and media. In Luanda many children now grow up with Portuguese as their first language. Demographers expect Africa's share of speakers to keep rising through this century.
Where it counts

Portuguese is also one of the most used languages online, usually ranked in the top ten for websites and social media, largely thanks to Brazil. It is not one of the six official languages of the United Nations, a status Portuguese-speaking countries have long asked for.
São Paulo state alone has about 45 million people, more than four times the population of Portugal.
Portugal is the birthplace of Portuguese, but its future is being written mostly in Brazil and Africa.

cards.text:
Portuguese has about 260 million speakers, which puts it among the ten most spoken languages on Earth.

About eight in ten live in Brazil. Portugal itself has only around 4% of the world's speakers, and Africa's share is the one growing fastest.

cards.title: European and Brazilian

deep.x: Sounds

Brazilians pronounce unstressed vowels clearly, while the Portuguese swallow many of them. In much of Brazil, t and d before an i sound become "tch" and "dj", so dia sounds like "djia". In Portugal, and in Rio de Janeiro, an s at the end of a syllable sounds like "sh".
Grammar

x: Ongoing actions: Portugal says "estou a ler", Brazil "estou lendo", for "I'm reading"
Pronoun position: Portugal says "chamo-me", Brazil usually "me chamo"
"You": in Portugal tu is for family and friends and você can sound distant; in most of Brazil você is the normal word, though tu survives in the south and parts of the north-east

deep.x: False friends

items.b: PT has a cold, BR constipated

deep.x: In writing, Angola, Mozambique and the other African countries generally follow the European standard, though each has its own accent, slang and local words.
Brazilian telenovelas, starting with Gabriela in 1977, made Brazilian accents and expressions familiar to a whole generation in Portugal.
Two standards, one language: the differences are real, but smaller than they first sound.

cards.text:
European and Brazilian Portuguese are one language with two standards, a little like British and American English.

They differ in pronunciation, some grammar, vocabulary and the everyday word for "you". Speakers understand each other well, with the occasional laugh over false friends.

cards.title: The 1990 spelling agreement

deep.x: Separate reforms in 1911 in Portugal, after the Republic, and in 1943 in Brazil put the two countries on different paths. A common agreement in 1945 failed because Brazil never applied it, and Portugal kept its own rules until the new agreement took effect.
What changed in Portugal

x: Silent consonants dropped: acção became ação, óptimo became ótimo, director became diretor
Months and seasons lost their capitals: Janeiro became janeiro
K, W and Y officially joined the alphabet, making 26 letters
Some hyphens went: hei-de became hei de

deep.x: What changed in Brazil

Brazil dropped the diaeresis, so lingüiça became linguiça, and some accents, so idéia became ideia and vôo became voo. By commonly cited estimates, the agreement changed about 1.5% of words in Portugal and about 0.5% in Brazil.

x: Consonant pronounced in Portugal, silent in Brazil
Portugal keeps facto, Brazil writes fato
Both spellings are correct

deep.x: Still unfinished

Angola has not ratified the agreement, and its use across Africa and in Timor-Leste is uneven. In Portugal, some writers, newspapers and citizens' groups still reject it, while supporters argue that a common spelling helps schools, dictionaries and international use.

deep.w: The agreement made Portuguese and Brazilian spelling identical
deep.r: Many differences remain, because spelling still follows each country's pronunciation

deep.x: The 1990 agreement brought the two spellings much closer, but not into one.

cards.text:
For most of the 20th century, Portugal and Brazil spelled many words differently.

The Orthographic Agreement, signed in Lisbon in 1990, set common rules for all Portuguese-speaking countries. It took decades to apply and is still debated, but schools and official texts in Portugal and Brazil now follow it.

cards.title: Sounds that puzzle learners

deep.x: Nasal vowels

Portuguese has five nasal vowels, made by letting air flow through the nose as well as the mouth, plus nasal diphthongs such as ão, õe and ãe. They are marked by a tilde or by an m or n closing the syllable. The difference changes meaning, so a learner who drops the nasal can say something quite different.
Vanishing vowels

In European Portuguese, unstressed vowels shrink or disappear. An unstressed e often vanishes completely, so telefone sounds close to "t'lefon'". An unstressed o turns into a u sound, so porto ends in "u". Strings of consonants result, which is why the language can sound clipped to outsiders.
Tricky letters

x: lh and nh sound like Italian gli and gn, as in filho and vinho
Initial r and rr are a throaty sound for most speakers, but some older people in the north and interior still roll them
In the Minho and much of the north, v and b often merge, so vinho can sound like "binho"
X can sound like "sh" (xadrez), "z" (exame), "ks" (táxi) or "s" (próximo)

deep.x: In parts of the Minho and Trás-os-Montes, some speakers still say ch as "tch", the way all Portuguese did in the Middle Ages, so chave sounds like "tchave".
European Portuguese is spoken far more compactly than it is written, and learning to hear the missing vowels is half the battle.

cards.text:
European Portuguese sounds softer and more compact than its spelling suggests; some foreigners even mistake it for a Slavic language.

Learners struggle with nasal vowels, unstressed vowels that almost vanish and a final s that sounds like "sh". The letter x alone has four different sounds.

quiz.q: Which Latin word became Portuguese "chave" (key)?
quiz.explain: Latin cl- at the start of a word turned into ch-.

quiz.q: Which language gave Portuguese aldeia, açúcar and almofada?
quiz.explain: Centuries of Muslim rule left hundreds of Arabic words, many starting with al- or a-.

quiz.q: In which language did medieval poets across Iberia write their love songs?
quiz.explain: Even Alfonso X of Castile wrote his Marian songs in it.

quiz.q: What does Portugal's "estou a ler" usually become in Brazil?
quiz.explain: Brazil uses the gerund for ongoing actions.

quiz.q: What did the 1990 agreement change in Portugal's spelling?
options: It dropped many silent consonants, as in ação
It made every spelling identical to Brazil's
quiz.explain: Acção became ação and óptimo became ótimo.

lessons.title: The Portuguese-speaking world
lessons.summary: The CPLP, nine countries, old outposts in Asia and the Portuguese diaspora.

cards.title: The CPLP

deep.x: The CPLP was founded on 17 July 1996 by seven countries: Portugal, Brazil, Angola, Mozambique, Cape Verde, Guinea-Bissau, and São Tomé and Príncipe. Its headquarters are in Lisbon, and its leaders meet at a summit every two years, with a rotating presidency.
What it does

x: Runs the International Institute of the Portuguese Language, based in Praia, Cape Verde
Coordinates cooperation on health, education, justice and election observation
Since a 2021 agreement signed in Luanda, eases visas and residence between members

deep.x: The newest member

Equatorial Guinea was a Spanish colony, but its islands of Bioko and Annobón were Portuguese until a 1778 treaty handed them to Spain, and Annobón still speaks a Portuguese-based creole. The country added Portuguese as an official language in 2010 and joined in 2014. One condition, abolishing the death penalty, was met with a 2022 law.
Strengths and limits

Members differ hugely in size, wealth and political system, and decisions need consensus. Critics see the CPLP as more a forum than a powerful organisation; supporters point to its role in Timor-Leste's independence and in crises in Guinea-Bissau. Dozens of countries, from Japan to Uruguay, have joined as associate observers.
Portugal used the 2021 mobility agreement to create a special CPLP residence permit, and tens of thousands of people from member countries applied within months.
The CPLP turns a shared language into a club of nine countries, loose but lasting.

cards.text:
The Community of Portuguese Language Countries, the CPLP, was founded in Lisbon in 1996. It now has nine members on four continents, home to about 300 million people.

It promotes the language, cooperation and easier movement between members, but it has no common market or army.

cards.title: Brazil

deep.x: For three centuries Brazil's wealth came from sugar, then from gold and diamonds in Minas Gerais in the 1700s, and later from coffee. Much of it was built on the labour of enslaved Africans: around 4 to 5 million were taken to Brazil, more than to any other country in the Americas. Brazil abolished slavery only in 1888, the last country in the Americas to do so.
The court in Rio

When Napoleon's army invaded Portugal in 1807, the royal family and much of the court sailed to Rio de Janeiro, which became the capital of the empire. In 1815 Brazil was raised to a kingdom equal to Portugal. After King João VI returned to Lisbon in 1821, his son Pedro stayed and declared independence on 7 September 1822, becoming Emperor Pedro I. He later returned to Portugal and, as Pedro IV, fought a civil war to win the throne for his daughter.
Ties today

x: Brazilians in Portugal number several hundred thousand, by far the largest foreign community
Millions of Brazilians have Portuguese ancestry, and many hold Portuguese passports
Brazilian music, from bossa nova to sertanejo, is part of everyday life in Portugal

deep.x: Rio de Janeiro is often described as the only city outside Europe ever to serve as the capital of a European empire, from 1808 to 1821.
Brazil began as Portugal's colony and grew into its giant sibling, with twenty times its population.

cards.text:
Brazil is by far the largest Portuguese-speaking country, with about 213 million people.

A Portuguese colony from 1500, it became independent in 1822 under a Portuguese prince. Today the ties run both ways: Brazilians are now the largest foreign community in Portugal.

cards.title: Angola

deep.x: The navigator Diogo Cão reached the mouth of the Congo river in 1482, and Luanda was founded in 1576. For centuries the colony was above all a source of enslaved people shipped to Brazil. Large-scale Portuguese settlement came only in the 20th century, and by 1974 a few hundred thousand settlers lived there.
Languages

Angola has many national languages, among them Umbundu, Kimbundu and Kikongo. Since independence, Portuguese has spread as the language of schools, cities and national unity. In the 2014 census about 70% of people said they spoke it, and in Luanda it is the home language of most families.
Oil and the economy

Oil makes up around nine-tenths of Angola's exports, so the economy rises and falls with world oil prices; diamonds come second. Angola left OPEC, the oil exporters' club, in 2024. Portuguese banks, builders and retailers are active there, and Angolan investors own stakes in Portuguese companies.
Culture
Angolan music crossed to Lisbon: kizomba and the fast electronic kuduro fill dance floors there, and slang such as "bué", meaning "loads", entered everyday Portuguese.
During Portugal's crisis in the early 2010s, Angola became a leading destination for Portuguese emigrants, reversing the flow of 1975.
Angola is a young, oil-rich country where Portuguese is turning from an official language into a mother tongue.

cards.text:
Angola, on Africa's south-west coast, is the second-largest Portuguese-speaking country by population, with about 37 million people.

Rich in oil and diamonds, it has rebuilt since a long civil war ended in 2002. Portuguese is spreading fast and is now the first language of many young Angolans.

cards.title: Mozambique

deep.x: Vasco da Gama called at Mozambique Island in 1498 on his way to India. The island, long the colonial capital, is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site. In 1898 the capital moved south to Lourenço Marques, renamed Maputo after independence.
Many languages

Emakhuwa is the most widely spoken first language, followed by languages such as Xichangana and Cisena. Portuguese works as the common language of government, schools and towns, and is the main language of most people in Maputo.
Neighbours and the Commonwealth

Surrounded mostly by English-speaking countries, Mozambique joined the Commonwealth in 1995. English is widely learnt for trade with South Africa, where generations of Mozambicans have worked in the mines.
Mozambicans and Portugal
Mozambique's flag is the only national flag that shows a modern rifle, crossed with a hoe and resting on a book.
Mozambique uses Portuguese as a common thread between dozens of languages, while looking to its English-speaking neighbours.

cards.text:
Mozambique stretches along Africa's south-east coast on the Indian Ocean, with about 34 million people.

Portuguese is the official language and a bridge between dozens of local languages, though only a minority speak it at home. It was also the first member of the Commonwealth that had never been a British colony.

cards.title: Cape Verde

deep.x: Portuguese navigators reached the islands around 1456–1462 and settled Santiago soon after. Ribeira Grande, now Cidade Velha, became the first European colonial town in the tropics and a major hub of the Atlantic slave trade. It has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2009.
Kriolu and morna

Kriolu grew from Portuguese and West African languages, and each island has its own variety. Morna, the slow, melancholy song made famous worldwide by Cesária Évora, the "barefoot diva" from São Vicente, was recognised by UNESCO as intangible heritage in 2019. Faster styles include funaná and coladeira.
A nation of emigrants

Droughts and famines, especially in the 1940s, drove many to leave. Large communities live around Boston in the United States, in Portugal, the Netherlands, France and Luxembourg. Money sent home is a big part of the economy, alongside tourism on beach islands such as Sal and Boa Vista.

x: Since multiparty elections began in 1991, governments have changed peacefully at the ballot box
The islands are dry: rain is scarce and much drinking water comes from desalination

deep.x: The name "Cape Verde", "green cape", refers to a headland near Dakar in Senegal, not to the islands, which are mostly dry and brown.
Ten dry islands, a creole language and a worldwide diaspora make Cape Verde a small country with a long reach.

cards.text:
Cape Verde is an archipelago of ten volcanic islands about 600 km off West Africa. It was uninhabited when the Portuguese arrived around 1460 and became a crossroads of the Atlantic.

People speak Kriolu at home and Portuguese at school, and more Cape Verdeans live abroad than on the islands.

cards.title: Guinea-Bissau and São Tomé

deep.x: Guinea-Bissau

Portuguese traders worked this coast from the 1440s, but control inland stayed weak for centuries. In 1956 Amílcar Cabral, an agronomist born in Bafatá, co-founded the PAIGC, which fought for the independence of both Guinea and Cape Verde. Cabral was assassinated in January 1973; the country declared independence that September, and Portugal recognised it in 1974.

Since independence the country has seen repeated coups and political crises. Most people farm, and cashew nuts are by far the main export. The Bijagós islands, where hippos swim in salt water, are a UNESCO biosphere reserve.
São Tomé and Príncipe

The islands were empty when the Portuguese arrived around 1470. Plantations of sugar, then cocoa and coffee, relied on enslaved and later contract workers from the mainland. In 1909 British chocolate makers led by Cadbury boycotted the islands' cocoa over conditions close to slavery.

x: The equator crosses Ilhéu das Rolas, an islet just south of São Tomé
With about 230,000 people, it is one of Africa's smallest countries
Forro and other creoles are spoken alongside Portuguese, which most people use

deep.x: In February 1953 colonial authorities killed hundreds of local people in the Batepá massacre; 3 February is now a national holiday in São Tomé.
Two small countries, one on the mainland and one at sea, both shaped by plantations, liberation and creole languages.

cards.text:
Guinea-Bissau, on the West African mainland, won independence after an armed struggle led by Amílcar Cabral's movement.

São Tomé and Príncipe, two small islands in the Gulf of Guinea, was once among the world's leading cocoa producers. In both countries, a Portuguese-based creole is the everyday language for many people.

cards.title: Timor-Leste

deep.x: The Portuguese arrived in the early 1500s, drawn by sandalwood. The island was later split with the Dutch, whose western half became part of Indonesia. As Portugal withdrew in 1975, the Fretilin movement declared independence, and Indonesia invaded nine days later and annexed the territory.
Occupation and resistance

Violence, famine and disease under the occupation cost an estimated 100,000 to 180,000 lives. The 1991 Santa Cruz massacre in Dili, filmed by a foreign journalist, drew world attention, and Bishop Carlos Belo and José Ramos-Horta shared the Nobel Peace Prize in 1996.
Portugal's cause

When the referendum of August 1999 was followed by militia violence, huge crowds in Portugal dressed in white, formed human chains and stopped for minutes of silence to demand international action. A UN-mandated force arrived that September.
Languages

Tetum is the main everyday language. Portuguese was chosen as co-official partly as a symbol of the resistance, which had used it. Indonesian and English are widely understood, and more than a dozen local languages are spoken.
The name means "East East": timur is Malay for east, and leste is Portuguese for east.
Timor-Leste kept Portuguese as a sign of its fight for independence, and Portugal backed that fight loudly.

cards.text:
Timor-Leste, the eastern half of the island of Timor, was Portuguese for about four centuries.

After 24 years of Indonesian occupation, its people voted for independence in 1999, and it became a state in 2002. Portuguese and Tetum are its official languages.

cards.title: Macau and Goa

deep.x: Macau

Portuguese traders settled Macau around 1557 with the consent of Chinese officials. For centuries it linked China, Japan and Europe and served as a base for missionaries. Under a 1987 agreement it was handed to China on 20 December 1999 as a Special Administrative Region, keeping its own laws and economy for 50 years, until 2049.

x: Portuguese is official alongside Chinese, though only a small fraction of residents speak it
The Historic Centre, with Senado Square's wavy calçada, has been a UNESCO site since 2005
Since 2003 China has used Macau as the venue of a trade forum with Portuguese-speaking countries

deep.x: Goa

Afonso de Albuquerque took Goa in 1510 and it became the capital of Portuguese Asia. In December 1961 Indian troops entered Goa, Daman and Diu, ending Portuguese rule; Portugal recognised this only after 1974. Konkani is the official language, and about a quarter of Goans are Catholic. Many Goans born before 1961, and their descendants, can register as Portuguese citizens.
Macau's famous egg tarts were popularised in 1989 by an English baker, Andrew Stow, who adapted the Lisbon pastel de nata.
Macau and Goa no longer speak much Portuguese, but they still eat, build and name things in a Portuguese way.

cards.text:
Macau, on China's south coast, was Portuguese for over 400 years until 1999, and Goa in India for over 450 years until 1961.

Few people there speak Portuguese today, but its legacy lives on in churches, street names, food, family names and law.

cards.title: The diaspora in Europe

deep.x: The great wave of the 1960s and 1970s built communities in France, Germany and Luxembourg. A second wave came after 2000, and especially during the crisis years of 2011–2014, when over 100,000 people a year left. Many were young graduates, and the UK became a leading destination until Brexit.
France

Counting children and grandchildren, France's Portuguese community is usually estimated at well over a million people. Portuguese surnames are common in French football, politics and business, and Portuguese is taught in some French state schools.
Switzerland and Luxembourg

In Switzerland, the Portuguese are one of the largest foreign communities, working in construction, hotels, cleaning and care. In Luxembourg they are the largest foreign nationality, and Portuguese is heard everywhere from building sites to bank offices.
Keeping in touch

x: Portuguese abroad elect four of the 230 MPs: two for Europe and two for the rest of the world
Community associations, Portuguese schools and RTP Internacional keep the language alive
Summer festivals in home villages fill up with returning families

deep.w: Emigration is a thing of the past
deep.r: Tens of thousands of Portuguese still leave each year, while Portugal now also receives many immigrants

deep.x: Portugal is a small country with a large second population spread across Europe.

cards.text:
About two million people born in Portugal live abroad, one of the highest shares of any European country.

Most are in Europe, above all in France, Switzerland, the United Kingdom and Luxembourg. Their children, the lusodescendentes, often keep the language and close ties to their parents' villages.

cards.title: The diaspora in the Americas

deep.x: Islanders had strong reasons to leave: tiny farms, earthquakes and eruptions, and few jobs. From the 1800s, Azorean men signed on to American whaling ships calling at Horta and Flores, and many settled in New Bedford, Massachusetts, then the whaling capital of the world.
United States

Massachusetts and Rhode Island hold the largest communities, around Fall River, New Bedford and Providence. The Ironbound district of Newark, New Jersey, is famous for its Portuguese restaurants and bakeries. In California's Central Valley, Azorean families built a large part of the dairy industry.
Canada and Venezuela

Organised emigration to Canada began in 1953, when the ship Saturnia landed Portuguese workers at Halifax. Toronto's Little Portugal and Montreal's Plateau grew from that wave. In Venezuela, tens of thousands of Madeirans ran shops, bakeries and supermarkets; since Venezuela's crisis of the 2010s, many have returned to Madeira.

x: Bermuda, Hawaii and South Africa also have long-established Portuguese communities
Azorean festivals of the Holy Spirit are celebrated from Massachusetts to California

deep.x: After the Capelinhos volcano erupted on Faial in 1957–58, a special US law let thousands of Azoreans emigrate to America.
From whaling ships to dairy farms, islanders from the Azores and Madeira carried Portugal deep into the Americas.

cards.text:
Across the Atlantic, Portuguese communities grew in Brazil, the United States, Canada and Venezuela, many of them from the Azores and Madeira.

About 1.3 million Americans and some 450,000 Canadians report Portuguese ancestry, from New England fishing towns to Toronto.

quiz.explain: A former Spanish colony with a Portuguese past on Annobón.

quiz.explain: It joined in 1995.

quiz.explain: Tetum is the main everyday language.
