options: The seabed gets deep close to shore
quiz.explain: Fixed foundations only suit shallow water.

lessons.title: Wildlife of Portugal
lessons.summary: Nature on our doorstep.

cards.title: A biodiversity hotspot
cards.text: Portugal sits in the Mediterranean hotspot, with Atlantic and Mediterranean influences, plus the unique islands of Madeira and the Azores.

deep.x: A **biodiversity hotspot** is a region with an unusually high number of species found nowhere else, which has also lost much of its original habitat. The Mediterranean Basin is one of about 36 hotspots worldwide, with around 25,000 plant species, roughly half of them endemic (found only there).
Portugal sits at a crossroads. Three of Europe's biogeographical regions meet within its borders.
Two climates, one small country
Mainland Portugal has more than 3,000 native plant species. Mountains, river valleys, estuaries and a long coastline add even more variety in a small space.
The islands

The Azores and Madeira belong to **Macaronesia**, a group of Atlantic archipelagos that also includes the Canaries and Cape Verde. Isolation has produced unique species: the Azores bullfinch (priolo), found only in the east of São Miguel, and Zino's petrel on Madeira, one of Europe's rarest seabirds.
The priolo fell to perhaps 40 pairs in the 1990s; restoring its native laurel forest helped it recover to around a thousand birds.
Portugal packs Atlantic, Mediterranean and island worlds into one small country, which makes it unusually rich in life.

cards.title: Peneda-Gerês
cards.text: Portugal's only national park, created in 1971, protects mountains, oak forests, Garrano horses, wolves and golden eagles.

deep.x: Peneda-Gerês National Park was created on 8 May 1971 and is still Portugal's only national park. It covers about 700 km² of granite mountains in the far north, between the Minho and Trás-os-Montes, along the border with Galicia.
Who lives there

The **Garrano** is an ancient breed of small, sturdy horse, adapted to steep slopes and harsh winters. Its herds live semi-wild and are a favourite target for wolves, which helps explain why the wolf survives here.
A layered landscape

Ancient oak woods, such as the Mata da Albergaria, shelter roe deer, martens and rare plants like the Gerês iris, which grows wild nowhere else. Stone villages, terraced fields and communal grazing are part of the park too; people have shaped this landscape for thousands of years.
The park also guards Roman roads, prehistoric burial mounds and the traditional granite granaries (espigueiros) of Soajo and Lindoso.

deep.w: Wolves in Gerês are a danger to hikers
deep.r: Iberian wolves avoid people; attacks on humans are virtually unknown in modern times

deep.x: Peneda-Gerês protects not just wild mountains, but a living landscape where wolves, wild horses and villagers share the hills.

cards.title: Laurisilva of Madeira
cards.text: Madeira's laurel forest is a relic of forests that covered Southern Europe millions of years ago. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1999.

deep.x: Twenty million years ago, much of southern Europe was covered by humid evergreen forest, with trees from the laurel family. As the climate cooled and dried during the ice ages, these forests vanished from the continent. They survived only on the Atlantic islands, where the ocean kept the climate mild and moist.
A forest that drinks clouds

The laurisilva grows on the misty north side of Madeira. Clouds pushed by trade winds drift through the trees, and droplets collect on leaves, moss and lichens and drip to the ground. This "fog capture" adds a lot of water to what falls as rain.
Much of that water ends up in Madeira's **levadas**, narrow irrigation channels built from the 1400s onward, which now double as famous walking trails.
What lives there

x: Trees such as til, vinhático and barbusano, all native to Macaronesia
The Madeira laurel pigeon (trocaz), found only in this forest
The Madeira firecrest, one of Europe's smallest birds
Hundreds of endemic insects, snails, mosses and ferns

deep.x: "Madeira" means "wood" in Portuguese. Early settlers cleared much of the forest by fire; the surviving laurisilva is the largest remaining in the world.
Madeira's laurel forest is a living fossil of Europe's ancient woodland, kept alive by Atlantic clouds.

cards.title: The Tagus estuary
cards.text: The Tagus estuary is one of Europe's most important wetlands for birds, hosting tens of thousands of waders and flamingos in winter.

deep.x: Where the Tejo meets the Atlantic, it spreads into a huge inner bay of about 300 km² before squeezing out through a narrow neck at Lisbon. Twice a day the tide drains away to reveal vast mudflats packed with worms, snails and small crustaceans: a buffet for birds.
A stop on a great flyway

The estuary lies on the **East Atlantic Flyway**, a bird migration route from the Arctic to West Africa. Some birds stop to refuel; others spend the whole winter here. In a typical winter, tens of thousands of waders use the estuary, with peak counts of all waterbirds above 100,000.
Why flamingos are pink

Flamingos eat tiny brine shrimp and algae rich in carotenoid pigments, the same family that colours carrots. Their bodies turn those pigments into pink feathers. A flamingo on a poor diet slowly fades to white.
Old salt pans, rice fields and reed beds around Alcochete, Samouco and the EVOA observatory are among the best places to watch. The Tagus Estuary Nature Reserve was created in 1976.
The Vasco da Gama Bridge, finished in 1998 and about 12 km long, was designed and built with measures to reduce disturbance to the birds of the estuary below.
On Lisbon's doorstep, the tide uncovers a feeding ground that keeps tens of thousands of migrating birds alive every winter.

cards.title: Dolphins of the Sado
cards.text: The Sado estuary near Setúbal has a resident population of bottlenose dolphins, one of the few in Europe, numbering around 30.

deep.x: Most bottlenose dolphins roam the open sea. The Sado estuary, between Setúbal and the Tróia peninsula, is different: it has a **resident** group that lives there year-round. Only a few places in Europe have resident estuarine dolphins, such as the Shannon estuary in Ireland.
A small, fragile family

Scientists have followed these dolphins since the 1980s and can recognise each one by the nicks and scars on its dorsal fin. The group fell from around 40 to the low 20s by the 2000s, and recent births have brought it back to around 30. With so few animals, every calf matters.

items.b: clicks to find fish in murky water

deep.x: Pressures
Dolphin-watching boats from Setúbal must follow a code: slow down, keep your distance, never surround the animals or chase them, and limit time spent nearby.
Each bottlenose dolphin develops its own signature whistle as a calf, and others can use it to call that individual, much like a name.
The Sado's resident dolphins are a rare, small family whose survival depends on how we share their busy estuary.

cards.title: The Berlengas
cards.text: The Berlengas archipelago off Peniche is a nature reserve and UNESCO biosphere reserve, home to seabird colonies and rich marine life.

deep.x: About 10 km off Peniche, the Berlengas are a rugged granite archipelago battered by Atlantic swell. The main island, Berlenga Grande, is less than 1.5 km long. The rest are rocky islets called the Estelas and the Farilhões.
Seabird city

Yellow-legged gulls boomed on scraps from fishing boats and landfills and crowded out other species. Managers have reduced their numbers to give rarer seabirds and plants room. The Berlengas were also once the southernmost breeding site of the common guillemot in Europe, though it has nearly disappeared.
Unique life

The islands have plants found nowhere else, such as a Berlengas sea-pink, and their own form of wall lizard. Underwater, the meeting of cold, nutrient-rich water and rocky reefs supports kelp, octopus, sea bream and colourful sea slugs, making it a top diving site.
Since 2019, only about 550 visitors a day may land on Berlenga Grande in summer, to protect its fragile soils and nesting birds.
The Berlengas show that a small, wild island can be both a seabird refuge and a visitor favourite, if access is carefully managed.

cards.title: Cork oaks
cards.text: Portugal is the world's largest cork producer, with roughly half of global output. Cork is stripped by hand every nine years without felling the tree.

deep.x: Cork is the bark of the cork oak (*Quercus suber*). The tree grows a thick, spongy outer bark to survive fire and drought. Remarkably, it can be stripped without harming the tree, which then grows a new layer.
A slow harvest

Skilled workers strip cork in early summer using axes, when the bark comes away cleanly. A cork oak can live about 200 years, giving around 15 harvests. The first two are too rough for stoppers; good wine corks come from the third stripping onward, when the tree is over 40.

x: First harvest at 25 years
next at 34, then at 43
wine-quality cork from about age 43

deep.x: Why cork works
Cork is made of tiny, sealed cells filled with air, coated in a waxy substance called suberin. That makes it light, waterproof, elastic and a superb insulator.
The montado

Cork oaks grow in open woodlands mixed with pasture, called **montado** in Portugal. This system supports cattle, black pigs, honey and a huge range of wildlife, including the Iberian imperial eagle and the Iberian lynx. It is illegal to fell a cork oak in Portugal without official permission.
The cork oak was declared Portugal's national tree in 2011.
Cork is a renewable harvest that keeps the tree alive and sustains one of Europe's richest farm landscapes.

cards.title: Forests and fire
cards.text: Large eucalyptus and pine plantations, abandonment of farmland and hotter summers have made wildfires a major threat. Native oaks burn less readily.

deep.x: Fire is a natural part of Mediterranean ecosystems, but Portugal's fires have grown more destructive. In 2017, more than 500,000 hectares burnt and over 100 people died, including 66 in the Pedrógão Grande fire in June.
Why the landscape changed

As people left rural villages from the 1960s onward, fields and pastures were abandoned and became dense scrub. Meanwhile, eucalyptus plantations for the paper industry spread fast, along with maritime pine. Eucalyptus is now the most common tree in Portugal's forests, covering roughly a quarter of the area.
Breaking the fire chain

Fires spread fastest across large, continuous blocks of flammable vegetation. A **mosaic** landscape, with farmland, grazing, native woodland and cleared strips around villages, gives fire fewer paths. Portugal now requires landowners to clear vegetation around houses and uses grazing herds and controlled burns in winter to reduce fuel.
Burning eucalyptus bark can peel away in long strips that are carried by the wind, starting new fires hundreds of metres ahead of the main front.
Fire risk is built into the landscape: abandoned land and continuous plantations become fuel when heatwaves arrive.

cards.title: Return of the vultures
cards.text: Griffon and black vultures have returned to the Douro International and Tejo International parks, thanks to feeding stations and protection.

deep.x: Vultures are nature's clean-up crew. A group of griffons can strip a dead sheep or deer in under an hour, removing carcasses that could otherwise spread disease.
How they nearly vanished

x: Poisoned bait set for wolves and foxes killed many vultures
Food shortages after 2001, when EU rules required farmers to remove dead livestock during the "mad cow" crisis
Disturbance near nesting cliffs

deep.x: The comeback

Rules were relaxed so farmers could leave carcasses at approved **feeding stations**. Poison was tackled with patrols and specially trained dogs. Nesting areas in the Douro International and Tejo International natural parks were protected.

The black vulture, Europe's largest bird of prey with a wingspan up to about 3 m, had stopped breeding in Portugal by the 1970s. It returned to breed in 2010 and now has several small colonies near the Spanish border. Griffons have also increased, and Egyptian vultures arrive in the Douro canyons each spring from Africa.
In South Asia, a cattle painkiller called diclofenac poisoned vultures feeding on carcasses and wiped out more than 95% of some species in the 1990s and 2000s.
Give vultures safe food and protect them from poison, and they return quickly to do their essential clean-up work.

cards.title: Where to see wildlife
cards.text: Gerês for wolves and horses, the Tagus estuary for flamingos, Sado for dolphins, Douro International for vultures and the Azores for whales.

deep.x: Portugal is small enough that you can see wolves' tracks in the morning and flamingos by evening, if you plan well. Timing and patience matter more than distance.
Best seasons
More places to try

x: Azores: sperm whales year-round from Pico, Faial and São Miguel; blue whales pass in spring
Ria Formosa near Faro: flamingos, spoonbills and chameleons in the pines
Castro Verde plains, Alentejo: great bustards and lesser kestrels
Berlengas: seabirds, plus diving on reefs

deep.x: Watch well
Wolves are best seen with a specialist guide, and even then often only through tracks, scats or a distant howl. Choose boat operators who follow the official whale and dolphin watching rules.
More than 20 species of whale and dolphin have been recorded around the Azores, making it one of the best places in Europe to see them.
Pick the right season and place, keep your distance, and Portugal's wildlife is closer than you think.

quiz.q: What is Portugal's only national park?
quiz.explain: Created in 1971.

quiz.q: How often is cork harvested from a tree?
quiz.explain: The tree survives.

lessons.title: Portuguese food
lessons.summary: Cod, sardines, convent sweets, olive oil, cheese, wine and coffee.

cards.title: The Atlantic diet

items: Slow stews shared at the table

deep.x: The name was popularised in the 2000s by doctors and nutritionists in Galicia and northern Portugal, to describe how people along the Atlantic edge of Iberia traditionally ate. It is less a set of rules than a portrait of a farming and fishing kitchen.
Built around the sea

Portugal eats more fish per person than any other EU country, about 55–60 kg a year, more than twice the EU average. Sardines, horse mackerel (carapau), hake, octopus and cod are everyday food, not luxuries.
Soup first

A typical meal still starts with soup: caldo verde, made from finely shredded couve galega (a dark leafy cabbage), potatoes and olive oil, or a simple vegetable purée. Bread is on every table, from the dense maize broa of the north to the wheat loaves of the Alentejo.

x: Pulses: chickpeas, broad beans and many kinds of bean
Seasonal vegetables, often from a family plot
Fruit for dessert, with sweets kept for feast days

deep.x: What science says

In 2024 a trial in Galicia found that families who followed the Atlantic diet for six months were less likely to develop metabolic syndrome, a cluster of risks for heart disease and diabetes. One study proves little on its own, but it fits a wider pattern: diets rich in fish, vegetables and olive oil tend to be healthy.

deep.w: Portuguese food is simply Mediterranean
deep.r: Portugal is included in UNESCO's Mediterranean diet listing, but it has no Mediterranean coast, and its cooking leans on the Atlantic

deep.x: The Atlantic diet is simple food from the sea and the garden, eaten slowly and together.

cards.text:
Portugal and Galicia share what nutritionists call the Atlantic diet: plenty of fish, vegetables, potatoes, bread and olive oil, with a little wine, eaten slowly with family.

It looks like the Mediterranean diet, but it leans more on the sea, on cabbage and potatoes, and on soups and stews cooked for hours.

cards.title: Bacalhau

deep.x: Cod lives in cold northern seas. Portuguese sailors were fishing the Grand Banks off Newfoundland soon after 1500. Salt cod suited a Catholic country with many meatless fast days and long sea voyages: it was cheap, light and very hard to spoil.
The White Fleet
Under the Estado Novo, cod fishing became a national campaign to make Portugal self-sufficient. From the 1930s the White Fleet, ships painted white, sailed north each spring for about six months.

x: Each fisherman fished alone from a tiny boat called a dóri, with hand lines
Fog, ice and storms made it one of Europe's most dangerous jobs
A hospital ship, the Gil Eannes, sailed with the fleet; it is now a museum in Viana do Castelo

steps: Dry in the sun at home

deep.x: The fleet faded in the 1970s, as countries extended their fishing zones to 200 nautical miles and cod stocks collapsed. Portugal now imports almost all its cod, much of it from Norway.
From the sea to the plate
Salt cod must be soaked (demolhado) for one to three days, changing the water often, before it is cooked.
Bacalhau à Brás is said to be named after Brás, a tavern keeper in Lisbon's Bairro Alto, though almost nothing is known about him.
Bacalhau is a fish from the far north turned into a Portuguese staple by salt, sun and centuries of habit.

cards.text:
Portugal's favourite fish doesn't live in Portuguese waters. Fishermen sailed to Newfoundland and Greenland to catch cod, salting it on board so it would keep for months.

Today most bacalhau comes from Norway and Iceland, but the Portuguese way of salting, drying and soaking it remains a national ritual.

cards.title: Sardines

deep.x: The sardine is a small, oily fish that swims in huge shoals along the Iberian coast. In spring it is thin; through the summer it feeds on plankton and builds up fat. Grilled whole over charcoal with coarse salt, it needs nothing else.
How to eat them

x: Lay a hot sardine on bread, often maize broa in the north
Eat with your fingers, lifting the flesh off the bones
Add a salad of tomato and roasted peppers, and boiled potatoes

deep.x: The canning towns

Canning arrived in the 19th century and boomed during the two world wars, when armies needed food that kept. Setúbal, Matosinhos, Portimão, Olhão and Peniche were lined with factories, where thousands of women cleaned and packed fish by hand on long shifts. Ramirez, founded in 1853, says it is the oldest canning company in the world still working.
Fewer fish, then more

Sardine numbers rise and fall naturally. In the 2010s stocks off Portugal and Spain fell so low that catches were tightly limited for several years. They have since recovered, but scientists and fishermen still watch the quotas closely.
Some fans age tins of sardines for years, like wine, turning them now and then, and say the fish grow softer and richer in the oil.
A sardine is at its best simply grilled in summer, and at its most lasting packed in olive oil.

cards.text:
Grilled sardines are the smell of a Portuguese summer. They are best from about June to October, when they are fat and oily, and are eaten on a slice of bread that soaks up the juices.

Portugal is also famous for tinned fish: canneries have packed sardines, tuna and mackerel in olive oil since the 19th century.

cards.title: Regional dishes

deep.x: Regional cooking follows the land. Where there is rain and grass, there are cows and cabbages; where there are cork-oak plains, there are black pigs; along the coast, there is fish.
North

Porto people are nicknamed tripeiros, "tripe eaters". Legend says that in 1415 the city gave all its meat to the fleet sailing to conquer Ceuta and kept only the offal, creating tripas à moda do Porto, a stew of tripe and white beans. The francesinha, a meat sandwich under melted cheese and a spicy beer-and-tomato sauce, appeared in Porto in the mid-20th century.
Centre
Bairrada, between Coimbra and Aveiro, is known for leitão: suckling pig roasted whole in wood ovens, with crisp skin and a peppery sauce, eaten with the region's sparkling wine.
South
Black Iberian pigs (porco preto) roam the Alentejo's montado, open woodland of cork and holm oaks, and fatten on acorns in autumn.
Islands

deep.w: Pork with clams comes from the Alentejo
deep.r: Despite its name, carne de porco à alentejana is often said to have been created on the coast, pairing Alentejo pork with Algarve clams

deep.x: Portuguese regional food is a map of the landscape: pasture, oak plains, coast and volcano.

cards.text:
Portugal is small, but each region cooks differently. The green, rainy north eats hearty soups, tripe and cured meats; the centre roasts suckling pig; the Alentejo makes bread soups and pork dishes; the Algarve cooks fish and shellfish.

The islands add their own: stews cooked in volcanic ground in the Azores, and beef skewers on bay-wood sticks in Madeira.

cards.title: Olive oil

deep.x: The word azeite comes from the Arabic az-zayt, "the oil". Olive trees have grown here since Roman times or earlier: an olive tree at Mouriscas, near Abrantes, has been estimated by researchers at over 3,000 years old, among the oldest in Europe.
Old groves and new
The Alqueva effect

The Alqueva dam on the Guadiana, completed in 2002, created one of Western Europe's largest artificial lakes and brought irrigation to the dry Alentejo. Hedgerow olive groves spread fast, and Portugal went from importing olive oil to exporting it. Critics worry about water use, pesticides and the loss of traditional landscapes.
Grades on the label

x: Acidity here measures free fatty acids, not sourness you can taste
Several regions, such as Trás-os-Montes and Moura, have protected-origin (DOP) oils
Light and heat spoil oil, so dark bottles and cool cupboards help

deep.w: You shouldn't fry with extra virgin olive oil
deep.r: Its smoke point, around 190–210 °C, is above normal frying temperatures, and it is quite stable when heated

deep.x: Portugal's olive oil boom joined ancient trees with modern irrigation, bringing real gains and real trade-offs.

cards.text:
Olive oil, azeite, is the fat of Portuguese cooking. It dresses fish and boiled potatoes, finishes soups and is poured generously over bacalhau.

Portugal has become one of the world's leading producers, mainly thanks to new irrigated groves in the Alentejo. Traditional varieties such as Galega and Cobrançosa give oils from mild to peppery.

cards.title: Cheese

deep.x: The thistle is the cardoon, a wild relative of the artichoke. Its dried purple flowers are soaked and crushed, and the liquid, rich in plant enzymes, curdles the milk. This method is rare outside Portugal and Spain.
How Serra da Estrela is made

It is made from late autumn to spring around the Serra da Estrela, mainland Portugal's highest range, from the milk of local sheep breeds. When ripe, the paste is so soft that the top crust is cut off like a lid and the cheese is scooped out with a spoon. Aged longer, as Serra da Estrela Velho, it becomes firm and sharp.
Across the country

x: Azeitão: small, creamy ewe's cheese from the Arrábida hills
Nisa and Évora: firmer ewe's cheeses from the Alentejo
São Jorge: a hard cow's milk cheese, sharp and peppery
Requeijão: a fresh whey cheese, often eaten with pumpkin jam

deep.x: The Azores have roughly as many cows as people and produce about a third of Portugal's milk, much of it from cows grazing outdoors all year.
In Portugal a wild thistle, not a calf's stomach, turns sheep's milk into some of Europe's most distinctive cheese.

cards.text:
Portugal's best-known cheeses are made from ewe's milk and set not with animal rennet but with the flowers of a wild thistle. The result is often soft, creamy and slightly bitter.

Serra da Estrela is the most famous, but Azeitão, Nisa, Évora and São Jorge from the Azores all have protected status.

cards.title: Convent sweets

deep.x: From the 15th century, sugar from Madeira and later Brazil made Portugal one of the first European countries where sugar was fairly plentiful. Convents had eggs from their farms, sugar from the trade, time and skill. They sold sweets to raise money or gave them to benefactors.
Names with a wink
When the convents closed

In 1834, after the Liberal Wars, religious orders for men were abolished and their property sold; convents for women could stay open until their last nun died. Recipes passed to families and bakeries. In 1837 a shop beside the Jerónimos Monastery began selling the custard tarts now known as pastéis de Belém, from a recipe still kept secret.
Nata or Belém?

Only the Belém shop can call its tarts pastéis de Belém; everywhere else they are pastéis de nata. Both have flaky, rolled pastry and a custard of egg yolks, milk and sugar, scorched in a very hot oven and dusted with cinnamon if you like.

x: Aveiro: ovos moles in shell-shaped wafers
Sintra: queijadas and travesseiros
Tentúgal, near Coimbra: paper-thin pastries filled with egg cream

deep.x: Ovos moles de Aveiro were the first Portuguese pastry to receive EU protected status, in 2008.
Portugal's sweets are the sweet side of history: sugar from the empire, eggs from the farm and patience from the cloister.

cards.text:
Many Portuguese sweets were born in convents and monasteries. Nuns and monks used egg whites to starch linen and clear wine, leaving mountains of yolks, which they mixed with sugar from Madeira and Brazil.

The results have heavenly names: toucinho do céu, papos de anjo, barriga de freira. The pastel de nata is the most famous heir of this tradition.

cards.title: Wine regions

deep.x: Vinho Verde

The region in the green north-west, demarcated in 1908, is one of the largest in Europe. Its best-known grape is Alvarinho, grown around Monção and Melgaço on the Minho river. Light, fairly low in alcohol and sometimes slightly fizzy, the wines suit fish and seafood.

deep.w: Vinho Verde is made from green grapes
deep.r: "Verde" means young: the wine is meant to be drunk fresh, and it can be white, red or rosé

deep.x: Douro

The Douro's vineyards climb steep schist slopes, cut into terraces by hand over centuries. Summers are very hot, and vine roots push deep into cracks in the rock to find water. Port is made here and traditionally aged in Vila Nova de Gaia, opposite Porto, while unfortified Douro reds and whites have become famous in their own right.
Alentejo
In the south, wide plains, hot summers and large estates give rich, fruity reds. The Alentejo also keeps a Roman method alive: vinho de talha, fermented in huge clay jars.
More to explore

x: Dão: elegant reds from granite hills
Bairrada: Baga reds and sparkling wines
Madeira and Setúbal: fortified and sweet wines

deep.x: The Portuguese drink more wine per person than almost any other nation, about 60 litres a year per adult.
Climate, soil and native grapes make Portugal's wine map one of the most varied in Europe.

cards.text:
Portugal packs very different wines into a small country. In the rainy Minho, Vinho Verde is light and fresh. Up the Douro valley, terraced schist slopes give port and powerful reds. On the hot Alentejo plains, wines are ripe and smooth.

Most are made from native grapes found almost nowhere else, such as Alvarinho, Touriga Nacional and Antão Vaz.

cards.title: Coffee culture

deep.x: Coffee became popular in Portugal in the 18th century, and the empire supplied it: Brazil, then São Tomé, Angola and Timor. In the early 1970s Angola was one of the world's largest producers, and its robusta beans shaped the strong Portuguese blend, which usually mixes arabica and robusta.
Beyond the bica
The Porto word cimbalino comes from La Cimbali, an Italian brand of espresso machine that spread through the city's cafés.
Historic cafés

x: A Brasileira (1905), in Chiado, with a bronze Fernando Pessoa at a table outside
Majestic (1921), on Porto's Rua de Santa Catarina, all mirrors and carved wood
Nicola, on Rossio, a writers' café since the 18th century, rebuilt in art deco style in 1929

deep.x: A coffee town

Campo Maior, in the Alentejo near the Spanish border, is home to Delta, Portugal's biggest coffee brand, founded by Rui Nabeiro in 1961. The town grew around roasting, and it now has a coffee science museum.

deep.w: "Bica" stands for "Beba Isto Com Açúcar"
deep.r: It's a popular story with no evidence; "bica" also means a spout, and the word's real origin is uncertain

deep.x: In Portugal coffee is less a drink than a short pause, taken standing up, many times a day.

cards.text:
In Portugal, um café means a short, strong espresso, drunk standing at the counter in a minute or two, often several times a day. In Lisbon it's a bica, in Porto a cimbalino.

Cafés and pastelarias are neighbourhood living rooms. Coffee is cheap, usually about €1 or less, and roasted in a dark, smooth style shaped by Portugal's links with Brazil and Africa.

cards.title: Tempura and beyond

deep.x: Portuguese traders first landed in Japan in 1543, on the island of Tanegashima. Nagasaki became their main port from 1571. For almost a century, until they were expelled in 1639, Portuguese merchants and Jesuit missionaries brought goods, guns and recipes.
The batter story

The most quoted origin of the name is the Latin quattuor tempora, Portuguese têmporas: four short seasons of fasting in the Church year, when fish and vegetables replaced meat. Other words have been suggested, such as tempero (seasoning), so the origin isn't certain. Japanese cooks later made the batter thinner and crisper.
Other traces in Japan
Around the world

x: Goa: vindaloo, from vinha d'alhos, a wine and garlic marinade
Macau: Macanese cooking mixes Portuguese, Chinese and Malay flavours
Malacca: Kristang families of Portuguese descent still cook "devil's curry"

deep.w: "Arigatō" comes from "obrigado"
deep.r: The Japanese word existed long before the Portuguese arrived; the likeness is a coincidence

deep.x: Portuguese sailors carried recipes as well as spices, and some, like tempura, became famous under new names.

cards.text:
Japanese tempura probably owes its start to Portuguese traders and missionaries, who reached Japan in the 1540s. They fried fish and vegetables in batter, much like Portugal's peixinhos da horta, battered green beans.

The name may come from têmporas, the Ember Days, when Catholics avoided meat. Portuguese cooking also left its mark in Goa, Macau, Malacca and Brazil.

quiz.q: What sets the milk for Serra da Estrela cheese?
quiz.explain: The cardoon thistle's flowers curdle the ewe's milk.

quiz.q: What does "verde" mean in Vinho Verde?
quiz.explain: It is a young wine and can be white, red or rosé.

quiz.q: Where did the White Fleet sail to catch cod?
quiz.explain: Cod lives in cold northern seas.

quiz.q: Which Japanese dish probably has Portuguese roots?
quiz.explain: Frying in batter arrived with Portuguese traders.

lessons.title: Music of Portugal
lessons.summary: Fado, cante, the song of 25 April and folk instruments.

cards.title: What fado is

items: One voice, often in a black shawl
Songs of fate, love and loss

deep.x: Nobody knows exactly how fado began. Most historians point to Lisbon in the 1820s–40s, in districts such as Alfama, Mouraria and Bairro Alto, among sailors, dockworkers and the taverns where they drank.
Many roots

The lundum and the modinha came from Brazil, especially after the royal court returned from Rio de Janeiro in 1821. The romantic idea that fado descends from Moorish songs is popular but has little evidence behind it.
Maria Severa

The first legendary fadista was Maria Severa (1820–1846), a singer from Mouraria whose love affair with an aristocrat, the Count of Vimioso, was retold in plays, a novel and Portugal's first sound film, A Severa (1931). By tradition, the black shawl many fadistas wear mourns her.
From taverns to the world

Records and radio carried fado across Portugal in the 20th century, and emigrants took it to Brazil, France and North America. The Fado Museum in Alfama opened in 1998, and UNESCO's listing in November 2011 recognised fado as a living tradition rather than a museum piece.

deep.w: Fado is always sad
deep.r: Many fados are cheeky, funny or joyful, like the fast fado corrido and songs in praise of Lisbon's neighbourhoods

deep.x: Fado is Lisbon's own song, born in its poor quarters and now heard around the world.

cards.text:
Fado is Lisbon's urban song: a single voice, with the Portuguese guitar and a classical guitar, singing of love, jealousy, poverty, the sea and fate. The word comes from the Latin fatum, destiny.

It grew in the city's poor riverside districts in the 19th century, and UNESCO added it to its list of intangible heritage in 2011.

cards.title: Fado houses

deep.x: Fado houses took their modern form in the 1930s, when performances moved from streets and taverns into licensed venues. Today Alfama, Mouraria and Bairro Alto have dozens of them, from tiny family taverns to elegant dining rooms. Some are run by fadistas themselves: the singer Argentina Santos ran Parreirinha de Alfama for decades.
House rules
The phrase you may hear before a song is "silêncio, que se vai cantar o fado": "silence, fado is about to be sung".

x: Talking during a song is a serious faux pas
Doors may be closed and waiters stand still
Applause comes at the end, never in the middle

deep.x: How a night works

A house usually has a resident guitarist and viola player and several singers, who each sing a short set of three or four fados before the next takes over. Late in the evening, staff, cooks and guests who sing may join in. Many singers of today began this way.

items: A set of 3–4 fados per singer
A pause to eat and talk
Late on, others may join in

deep.x: Many fado houses charge a minimum spend instead of a ticket, so the dinner pays the musicians.
In a fado house the music comes first: dinner pauses, the room goes dark and everyone listens.

cards.text:
The classic place to hear fado is a casa de fado, a small restaurant where singers take turns between courses. When the lights dim, waiters stop serving and the room falls silent.

In fado vadio, "vagrant fado", amateurs stand up to sing in neighbourhood taverns, keeping the tradition alive away from the tourist trail.

cards.title: Lisbon and Coimbra

deep.x: Lisbon's fixed fados

Traditional Lisbon fado uses a repertoire of a few hundred named melodies. A singer chooses a melody and a poem with the right rhythm and metre, so the same tune can carry hundreds of different lyrics. The three oldest, the fado menor, fado corrido and fado mouraria, are often called the "castiço" (true-born) fados.
The art of bending a tune
Lisbon singers talk of estilar: stretching, delaying and ornamenting the melody differently every time, so no two performances are alike. The musicians must follow every pause.
Coimbra's songs

In Coimbra, songs were usually written by named composers and sung closer to the page, like a Romantic art song. They follow the academic year, above all the Queima das Fitas in May, when finishing students burn the ribbons of their faculty colours.
Many Coimbra musicians prefer the name "canção de Coimbra", Coimbra song, to stress that it is its own tradition.

deep.w: Coimbra fado is Lisbon fado sung by students
deep.r: It has its own repertoire, composers and guitar tuning, and grew out of Romantic song rather than tavern fado

deep.x: Lisbon fado reinvents old tunes with new words; Coimbra fado sings composed songs of student life.

cards.text:
Fado has two homes. In Lisbon, singers often set new poems to a stock of traditional melodies, such as the fado menor or fado corrido, and phrase them freely.

Coimbra's fado grew in its university: composed songs sung by men at night, tied to student life, farewells and the city itself.

cards.title: Guitarra and viola

deep.x: Fado musicians rarely read sheet music. A guitarist must know hundreds of fados by ear and follow a singer who may hold a note, speed up or drop out without warning. Players describe it as a conversation more than an accompaniment.
Who does what
The guitarra never plays over the words. It answers in the gaps between lines, echoes a phrase or adds a short run before the next verse. Good accompanists make a singer sound freer, not busier.
Guitar on its own
Players to know

x: Raul Nery and José Fontes Rocha were mid-20th-century masters, Fontes Rocha long playing for Amália
António Chainho took the guitarra into jazz and world music
Marta Pereira da Costa is among the first women to play it professionally on world stages

deep.x: Guitarras are still largely handmade in small workshops in Lisbon and Coimbra, and a good one can take weeks to build.

deep.w: The fado "viola" is the bowed orchestral instrument
deep.r: In Portugal "viola" is the everyday word for the six-string guitar; the orchestral viola is a "violeta"

deep.x: Fado is a conversation in three parts: the voice speaks, the guitarra replies, the viola holds the ground.

cards.text:
In fado, "guitarra" means the pear-shaped Portuguese guitar, while "viola" is the ordinary six-string guitar. The guitarra answers the singer's lines; the viola keeps the harmony and pulse.

The players follow the singer closely, since melodies stretch and pause. Instrumental pieces called guitarradas let the guitarra shine on its own.

cards.title: Amália Rodrigues

deep.x: Amália made her professional debut in 1939 at the Retiro da Severa, a Lisbon fado house. Within a few years she was the city's best-paid fadista, touring Brazil and starring in films.
A singer of poets

Amália chose lyrics by major poets, from Camões to David Mourão-Ferreira, Pedro Homem de Mello and Alexandre O'Neill. From 1962 the French-born composer Alain Oulman wrote melodies for her that broke with the traditional fado forms. Some purists objected; most now see it as a turning point.
Fame abroad

The French film Les Amants du Tage (1955) featured her singing, and in 1956 she played the Olympia in Paris. She went on to tour Europe, the Americas, the Soviet Union and Japan, singing in several languages.
Politics and memory

Because she was famous under the dictatorship, some accused her after 1974 of being the regime's singer. Later accounts say she quietly helped opponents of the regime, and historians still debate her politics.
When she died in October 1999, during an election campaign, the government declared three days of national mourning. In 2001 she became the first woman laid to rest in the National Pantheon.
Her house on Rua de São Bento, in Lisbon, is now a museum, kept much as she left it.
Amália made fado international by pairing a unique voice with great poetry and new music.

cards.text:
Amália Rodrigues (1920–1999) took fado from Lisbon's taverns to concert halls across the world. Born into a poor family, she sold fruit on the Lisbon docks as a girl before her voice made her a star.

She sang great poets, worked with composers who widened fado's sound, and remains the voice most people link with Portugal.

cards.title: Fado and censorship

deep.x: After the military coup of 1926, the new authorities brought in prior censorship of shows, and from 1927 fado lyrics had to be submitted for approval. Over time, rough tavern songs about crime, prostitution and injustice faded, replaced by songs about love, Lisbon and the nation.
Licensed and controlled

x: Professional fadistas needed a carteira profissional, an official card
Performances moved into registered houses with set programmes
Radio, and later television, spread a polished, approved style

deep.x: "Fado, Fátima, football"

Critics summed up the regime's culture as the "three Fs": fado, Fátima and football, supposedly used to keep people content. Historians see this as a simplification. Some officials disliked fado as gloomy and low-class, and the shrine and the sport had lives of their own.
After the revolution

In the years after 1974, protest songs and new pop dominated, and fado seemed old-fashioned. Singers such as Carlos do Carmo showed it could carry modern, socially aware poetry, and by the 1990s a new generation brought it back.
Censorship tamed fado for half a century, but the genre outlived both the regime and the stigma.

cards.text:
Under the dictatorship, fado lyrics had to be approved by censors before being sung in public, and professional singers needed an official licence. Fado moved from the streets into licensed fado houses.

The regime favoured a tidy, patriotic fado, and after 1974 some saw it as the old regime's music. It took years for fado to lose that label.

cards.title: Cante alentejano

deep.x: Cante belongs to everyday life as much as to the stage. Men gathered in taverns after work and began to sing, one voice at a time, until the whole room joined in. In mining towns such as Aljustrel, singing together was a way of holding a hard-working community together.
Passed on by ear

Most groups are village choirs or local associations. Men often perform in traditional farm workers' clothes, with hats, waistcoats and boots. A single moda can last several minutes with only a few lines of text, stretched out and repeated.
Saving a tradition

By the late 20th century, as villages emptied and farm work was mechanised, cante seemed to be ageing with its singers. Towns in the region prepared the UNESCO bid, and the listing brought new attention and pride.

x: More women's and mixed choirs have formed
Schools in the region have run cante classes
Pop, jazz and fado musicians have recorded with cante groups

deep.x: Serpa, Beja and other Alentejo towns hold regular cante festivals, and Serpa has a house dedicated to the tradition, the Casa do Cante.
Cante survived because communities chose to keep singing it, now with new voices joining in.

cards.text:
Cante alentejano, the unaccompanied group singing of the Alentejo, joined UNESCO's list in 2014. Its songs, called modas, are slow and spacious, like the plains they come from.

Once sung in fields, mines and taverns, cante now lives in choirs, festivals and schools, and young groups mix it with new music.

cards.title: Grândola, Vila Morena

deep.x: José Afonso (1929–1987), known as Zeca, began as a Coimbra singer and became the leading voice of Portuguese protest song. Many of his songs were banned from radio, and he was arrested by the political police in 1973.
The song

Afonso wrote it as a tribute to the town of Grândola, where he had sung in 1964 for a workers' music society. It describes a sun-browned town of fraternity and equality, where the people have the final say, set to a slow melody in the spirit of cante. It came out on the album Cantigas do Maio (1971), recorded in France. Instead of instruments, it opens with the crunch of marching feet on gravel.
Two songs, two signals

The first signal, at 22:55 on 24 April, was Paulo de Carvalho's "E Depois do Adeus", Portugal's Eurovision entry that year. A harmless love song was a safe choice. "Grândola", by a singer the regime distrusted, confirmed that the operation was going ahead.
By the next day, crowds filled the streets and handed carnations to soldiers, who put them in their rifles.
In 2013, protesters in the public gallery interrupted the prime minister in parliament by singing "Grândola", showing it is still a living protest song.
A slow song about a small town became the sound of Portugal's return to democracy.

cards.text:
Just after midnight on 25 April 1974, Rádio Renascença played José Afonso's "Grândola, Vila Morena". It was the second signal for army officers to begin the coup that ended 48 years of dictatorship.

The song, about brotherhood and equality in an Alentejo town, became the anthem of the Carnation Revolution and is still sung at every 25 April celebration.

cards.title: Folk instruments

deep.x: From cavaquinho to ukulele

The cavaquinho, a tiny four-string guitar from the Minho, travelled with emigrants. In 1879 Madeiran workers arrived in Hawaii aboard the ship Ravenscrag, bringing a similar island instrument, the machete or braguinha. Madeiran woodworkers began building them in Honolulu, and Hawaiians adopted it as the ukulele.
A guitar for every region

x: Viola braguesa: Minho, with ten strings in five pairs
Viola campaniça: Alentejo, used for improvised sung duels
Viola da terra: Azores, with two heart-shaped sound holes

deep.x: Drums and pipes

The adufe is a square frame drum of goatskin, sometimes with seeds or pebbles inside that rattle. It is played mainly by women in Beira Baixa villages such as Monsanto. In Trás-os-Montes, the gaita-de-foles bagpipe leads dances and processions, and in the north the Zés Pereiras, groups of big drums, open village festivals.
Folk groups and collectors recorded old players in the late 20th century, and today's musicians mix these instruments with rock, jazz and electronics.
Idanha-a-Nova, home of the adufe, joined UNESCO's network of Creative Cities of Music in 2015.
Portugal's folk instruments are small, local and portable, and one of them became the ukulele.

cards.text:
Beyond fado, Portuguese folk music uses a family of local instruments: the small cavaquinho, regional guitars called violas, bagpipes in the north-east and square drums in the Beira.

Each region has its own sound. Many of these instruments nearly vanished in the 20th century and have been revived by folk groups and young musicians.

cards.title: Music today

items: New fado: young voices, new poets

deep.x: From the late 1990s, singers such as Mariza, Camané, Ana Moura and Carminho made fado popular again, at home and on international stages. Some stay close to tradition; others add piano, strings, electronics or pop songwriters.
Lisbon as a lusophone hub

Many thousands of people with roots in Angola, Cape Verde, Guinea-Bissau, São Tomé and Brazil live around Lisbon, and their music has shaped the city's sound. In the 2000s, Lisbon producers mixed Angolan kuduro with electronic dance music and took it to clubs around the world.
Singing in Portuguese

For a while many Portuguese pop bands sang in English. Hip hop in Portuguese grew from the 1990s, and in 2017 Salvador Sobral won Eurovision, Portugal's first victory, with a quiet ballad in Portuguese. Many listeners saw it as proof that the language could travel.
Summer festivals, from big rock events to folk gatherings in small towns, now give all these styles a stage side by side.

deep.w: Fado is only for older listeners
deep.r: Many of today's fadistas began singing as teenagers, and fado concerts and fado houses draw audiences of all ages

deep.x: Portuguese music now moves freely between fado, Africa, Brazil and global pop, in its own language.

cards.text:
Portuguese music today mixes old and new. Since the late 1990s, a generation of fadistas has brought fado back to young audiences, often with new instruments and poets.

Lisbon is also a hub for sounds from Angola, Cape Verde and Brazil, while pop, rap and folk artists sing in Portuguese with growing confidence.

quiz.explain: It was inscribed in November 2011.

quiz.q: What did "Grândola, Vila Morena" signal on 25 April 1974?
options: The go-ahead for the military coup
quiz.explain: Rádio Renascença played it just after midnight.

quiz.q: Which instrument became the Hawaiian ukulele?
quiz.explain: Madeiran workers brought it to Hawaii in 1879.

quiz.q: In fado, what is the "viola"?
quiz.explain: It keeps the chords and the rhythm.

lessons.title: Portuguese culture
lessons.summary: Traditions, crafts and icons.

cards.title: Portuguese guitar
cards.text: The Portuguese guitar has 12 strings in six pairs and a pear-shaped body, giving fado its shimmering sound. Carlos Paredes made it famous as a solo instrument.

deep.x: The Portuguese guitar descends from the European cittern, a pear-shaped instrument with metal strings. In the 18th century the so-called "English guitar", popular with Porto's British merchant community, became fashionable, and Portuguese makers adapted it. By the late 19th century it had become the voice of fado.
Why it shimmers

x: **12 steel strings in 6 pairs** (courses): each pair is plucked together, so notes ring with a slight chorus
The lower pairs are tuned an octave apart, adding a bright overtone
It's played with the thumb and index finger, often with picks called **unhas** ("nails"), in a fast technique called dedilho
A fan of screw tuners on the head replaces the usual wooden pegs

deep.x: The fado line-up

In a fado house you'll usually see three musicians: the singer, the Portuguese guitar weaving a counter-melody, and the **viola** (a classical guitar) keeping the chords. A bass guitar is often added.
Carlos Paredes

Carlos Paredes (1925–2004) came from a Coimbra family of players; his father, Artur Paredes, was already famous. His 1967 album *Guitarra Portuguesa* showed the instrument could stand alone, with no singer at all. During the dictatorship he was jailed for political activity, and he kept working as a hospital clerk for most of his life.
Twelve strings in pairs give the Portuguese guitar its trembling, silvery voice: half harp, half mandolin.

cards.title: Coimbra fado
cards.text: Coimbra fado is sung by men, traditionally students in black capes, often as serenades. It's more lyrical and academic than Lisbon fado.

deep.x: Coimbra has one of Europe's oldest universities: founded in 1290 and settled in Coimbra for good in 1537. Its students developed their own song tradition in the 19th century, and Coimbra fado is still tied to student life, sung by men in the academic dress of black cape and suit (capa e batina).
The serenade

The classic setting is a night serenade: a singer and guitarists under a window, or on the steps of the Old Cathedral (Sé Velha). The songs are often addressed to a sweetheart, to the city, or to the student years that will soon end.
No clapping, please
At a serenade, the audience traditionally doesn't applaud. Instead, people show approval by clearing their throats or coughing softly. Students sometimes wave or flick the edges of their capes.
From love songs to protest

In the 1960s, Coimbra students such as José Afonso (Zeca Afonso) took the serenade style and turned it into the **balada**, simpler songs with political messages. This became the root of the protest music that accompanied the fall of the dictatorship in 1974.

x: Augusto Hilário (1864–1896) is remembered as an early star of the genre
The University of Coimbra was listed by UNESCO in 2013

deep.x: The Coimbra guitar is tuned a whole tone lower than the Lisbon guitar, which gives Coimbra fado its darker, mellower colour.
Coimbra fado is a student's goodbye set to music: sung at night, received with a cough instead of applause.

cards.title: Azulejo museum
cards.text: Lisbon's National Azulejo Museum, in the Madre de Deus convent, shows five centuries of tiles, including a 23-metre panorama of Lisbon before the 1755 earthquake.

deep.x: The word **azulejo** comes from the Arabic *az-zulayj*, "polished little stone", not from *azul* (blue). Glazed tiles arrived through Moorish Spain, and from the 16th century Portugal used them more than almost any other country: on church walls, palaces, stations and house fronts.
A convent full of tiles

The museum sits in the Convent of Madre de Deus, founded in 1509 by Queen Leonor, widow of King João II. The museum opened in 1965 and became independent in 1980. Its gilded church and cloisters are part of the visit.
Five centuries in one building

x: Early tiles used the **corda seca** method: lines of grease and manganese kept the coloured glazes apart
Later, the Italian majolica technique let painters work on a flat white glaze, like a canvas
From about 1700, Dutch-influenced **blue on white** panels told stories across whole walls
After the 1755 earthquake, simple patterned tiles were mass-produced to rebuild Lisbon quickly

deep.x: The Great Lisbon Panorama

The museum's star is a panel about 23 m long showing the Lisbon waterfront around 1700: the royal palace, churches and ships. Almost all of it was destroyed in 1755, so this is one of the best views of the lost city.

deep.w: Azulejo means "blue tile"
deep.r: The word comes from Arabic for "polished stone"; early tiles were green, ochre and other colours

deep.x: Portugal turned the humble tile into a public art: walls that tell stories, protect from damp and reflect the light.

cards.title: Calçada portuguesa
cards.text: Portugal's black and white stone pavements are laid by hand by calceteiros. The waves of Rossio square inspired Copacabana's promenade in Rio.

deep.x: Portuguese pavement is made of small, roughly cubic stones, about 4–6 cm across, set by hand into sand and tapped down with a hammer. White limestone and black basalt are arranged into patterns, from simple waves to ships, stars and coats of arms.
How it started

The modern tradition began in 1842 at Lisbon's São Jorge Castle, where military engineer Eusébio Furtado had prisoners pave a parade ground in a zigzag. Around 1848–49, Rossio square received its famous wavy design, called **Mar Largo** ("wide sea").
Across the ocean

Portuguese workers took the craft to Brazil. Copacabana's beach promenade in Rio copied Rossio's waves, but turned them to run parallel to the sea. In 1970 the landscape architect Roberto Burle Marx widened the promenade and designed new patterns, keeping the waves. You can also find calçada in Macau, Mozambique and Cape Verde.
A craft under pressure

x: Calceteiros are fewer each year; Lisbon has run a school for them since 1986
The stones get slippery when wet and can be hard for wheelchairs, prams and high heels
Many cities now mix calçada with smoother strips to make walking safer

deep.x: Lisbon's calçada has been described as one of the largest pieces of public art in Europe: an artwork people walk on every day.
Calçada turns a pavement into a picture, one hand-placed stone at a time.

cards.title: Filigree
cards.text: Portuguese filigree, especially from Gondomar and Póvoa de Lanhoso, twists fine gold and silver threads into delicate jewellery, like the heart of Viana.

deep.x: Filigree comes from the Latin *filum* (thread) and *granum* (grain). It's an ancient technique, found in jewellery from Mesopotamia, Etruria and Iron Age Iberia. In Portugal it became a living folk art, concentrated in the north.
How it's made

The craftsperson first makes a strong outline frame, then fills it with tiny coils of twisted, flattened wire, like stained glass made of metal. Finally the piece is soldered, cleaned and polished. A single pair of earrings can take days.

items.b: heart with a flame on top

deep.x: Where it lives

x: **Gondomar**, near Porto, has the largest concentration of goldsmiths and filigree workshops
**Póvoa de Lanhoso**, near Braga, has a long filigree tradition of its own
**Viana do Castelo** made the heart famous; at the Romaria da Senhora d'Agonia in August, women in traditional dress parade wearing layers of gold

deep.x: The heart of Viana
The heart design is linked to devotion to the Sacred Heart of Jesus, encouraged by Queen Maria I in the late 18th century. Today it's sold worldwide as a symbol of Portugal and of love.
Traditional Portuguese gold jewellery is often 19.2 carat (800 parts per 1,000), purer than the 18 carat standard common elsewhere in Europe.
Filigree is lace made of gold: thousands of hair-thin twists held in a strong frame.

cards.title: Festas populares
cards.text: In June, cities celebrate saints: Santo António in Lisbon with grilled sardines and basil pots, São João in Porto with plastic hammers and leeks.

deep.x: June is Portugal's month of saints. The festivals honour **Santo António** (13 June), **São João** (24 June) and **São Pedro** (29 June). They fall around the summer solstice, and many customs, like bonfires and fresh herbs, probably go back to older midsummer celebrations.
Lisbon: Santo António

Saint Anthony was born in Lisbon around 1195 and died in Padua in 1231, which is why Italians call him Anthony of Padua. He's seen as a matchmaker, so the city still hosts the **Santo António weddings**.

x: Neighbourhoods compete in the **Marchas Populares**, parading down Avenida da Liberdade
Alfama and Bica fill with grilled sardines, bread, wine and music
Lovers give a **manjerico**, a small pot of basil with a paper carnation and a short four-line verse

deep.x: Porto: São João

On the night of 23 June, Porto barely sleeps. People hit each other gently on the head with squeaky plastic hammers, a custom from the 1960s that replaced the older habit of waving garlic flowers or leeks under people's noses. At midnight, fireworks light up the Douro.
You're not supposed to sniff a manjerico directly: tradition says you stroke it with your hand and smell your palm.
Portugal's June saints are an excuse for a whole country to eat outdoors, dance and stay up late.

cards.title: Barcelos rooster
cards.text: The Barcelos rooster legend tells of a pilgrim wrongly accused of theft; a roasted rooster crowed to prove his innocence. It became a national symbol.

deep.x: The story is set in medieval times. A pilgrim from Galicia, on his way to Santiago de Compostela, stopped in Barcelos just as a theft had shocked the town. As a stranger, he was arrested and sentenced to hang.
The miracle

He asked to see the judge, who was sitting down to dinner with a roasted rooster on his plate. The pilgrim declared that, as surely as he was innocent, the rooster would crow. The judge laughed, but when the pilgrim was about to be hanged, the bird stood up on the plate and crowed. The judge rushed to save him.
From legend to souvenir

A 14th-century stone cross linked to the legend, the Cruzeiro do Senhor do Galo, is kept at the archaeological museum in Barcelos. The colourful ceramic rooster, black with red hearts and flowers, is much more recent.

x: In the 1930s–50s, the Estado Novo's propaganda office promoted folk crafts as symbols of the nation
The rooster became the face of Portuguese tourism and of countless tea towels
Barcelos still holds one of Portugal's biggest weekly markets, every Thursday

deep.x: A very similar miracle is told in Santo Domingo de la Calzada in Spain, on the same pilgrim route, where a live hen and rooster are still kept inside the cathedral.
A folk miracle about justice became, thanks to clever 20th-century promotion, the best-known emblem of Portugal.

cards.title: Literature beyond Camões
cards.text: Fernando Pessoa, Eça de Queirós, Sophia de Mello Breyner and José Saramago are pillars of Portuguese literature.

deep.x: Camões gave Portugal its epic in 1572, but the country's literature kept renewing itself. Four writers show its range: a realist novelist, a modernist poet of many selves, a poet of the sea and light, and a Nobel novelist.
The four pillars

x: **Eça de Queirós** (1845–1900): sharp, ironic realist novels such as *The Crime of Father Amaro* (1875) and *The Maias* (1888), a portrait of Lisbon's decaying upper class. He wrote much of it while working as a consul in England and France.
**Fernando Pessoa** (1888–1935): wrote under dozens of invented authors, his **heteronyms**, each with a biography and style. *The Book of Disquiet* was only published in 1982.

**Sophia de Mello Breyner Andresen** (1919–2004): clear poems about the sea, light and justice, plus children's classics like *A Menina do Mar*. In 1999 she was the first woman to win the Camões Prize.

**José Saramago** (1922–2010): long sentences, little punctuation and big "what if" ideas, as in *Blindness* (1995). He won the Nobel Prize in 1998, still the only one for a Portuguese-language writer.

deep.x: Where to start
Try a Sophia short story, Eça's *The Maias*, or Saramago's *Memorial do Convento* (1982), set around the building of the Mafra palace.
In 2014 Sophia's remains were moved to Lisbon's National Pantheon, an honour given to very few writers.
Portuguese literature moves from irony to multiplicity to clarity to fable, and every one of these writers is still widely read.

cards.title: Cante alentejano
cards.text: Alentejo's polyphonic choral singing, without instruments, was inscribed by UNESCO in 2014. Groups of men or women sing slow, deep songs about the land.

deep.x: Cante is the traditional group singing of the Alentejo, the vast plain of southern Portugal. It's sung without instruments, slowly, by groups of about ten to thirty singers standing in rows. UNESCO added it to its list of intangible heritage in November 2014.
How a song unfolds
The **ponto** starts the song alone. The **alto** then takes over the line, singing higher, and the whole choir enters in harmony. The alto's voice floats above the group, decorating the melody.
Songs of work and land

Cante grew among farm workers, miners and villages. Songs talk about the land, the wheat fields, the heat, love, longing and hard labour. Singers often link arms and sway with a slow step as they sing, as if walking together.

x: Men's groups dominated for most of the 20th century; women's and mixed groups have grown since
Its origins are debated: church chant, Arab music and older folk singing have all been suggested
Towns like Serpa, Beja and Cuba hold regular festivals

deep.x: The song that gave the signal for the Carnation Revolution on 25 April 1974, José Afonso's "Grândola, Vila Morena", was inspired by the Alentejo's choral style.
Cante is a whole village singing as one voice, with a single high line floating above the crowd.

cards.title: The language
cards.text: Portuguese is spoken by about 260 million people across four continents, the most spoken language in the Southern Hemisphere.

deep.x: Portuguese grew out of the spoken Latin of the Roman province of Gallaecia, in what is now northern Portugal and Galicia. Medieval Galician-Portuguese was the language of lyric poetry across Iberia. The oldest dated royal document is King Afonso II's will of 1214, and King Dinis made Portuguese the official language of the court around 1290.
Who speaks it
Portuguese is official in nine countries: Portugal, Brazil, Angola, Mozambique, Cape Verde, Guinea-Bissau, São Tomé and Príncipe, East Timor and Equatorial Guinea, plus Macau.
Layers in the words

x: **Latin** gives the core: *pão*, *água*, *mãe*
**Arabic** left hundreds of words, often starting with *al-* or *a-*: *azeite*, *arroz*, *alface*
Exploration brought words from Tupi, Kimbundu and Asian languages: *ananás*, *jacaré*

deep.x: Hard bits for learners

Nasal vowels (*pão*, *mãe*) and the swallowed unstressed vowels of European Portuguese make it tricky to hear. Brazilian Portuguese keeps more vowels, so many Portuguese understand Brazilians more easily than the reverse.
The 1990 Orthographic Agreement aimed to unify spelling across Portuguese-speaking countries; Portugal adopted it fully in 2015, but debate continues.
Portuguese left a small corner of Europe and became a language of about 260 million people on four continents.

quiz.q: How many strings does the Portuguese guitar have?
quiz.explain: Six pairs.

quiz.q: Which city celebrates São João with plastic hammers?
quiz.explain: On the night of 23–24 June.

lessons.title: Building Portugal
lessons.summary: From Romanesque cathedrals to Manueline, Pombaline and the Porto School.

cards.title: Romanesque churches

deep.x: Romanesque arrived from France with Burgundian nobles and monks, including Count Henry of Burgundy, father of the first king, and along the pilgrim routes to Santiago de Compostela. The granite north has the most examples.
Fortress cathedrals

Lisbon's cathedral was begun soon after Afonso Henriques took the city in 1147. Coimbra's Old Cathedral, started around 1162, is one of the best-preserved Romanesque cathedrals in Portugal, its crenellated walls ready for a siege.
Village churches

In the valleys of the Sousa, Tâmega and Douro, east of Porto, dozens of small Romanesque churches, monasteries and bridges are linked in a tourist route, the Rota do Românico, with 58 monuments. Carvings around their doors show animals, monsters and knots, symbolic rather than realistic.
A rare town hall
The Domus Municipalis in Bragança, a five-sided building over a water cistern, is one of very few civic buildings in Romanesque style surviving in the Iberian Peninsula.
On many granite churches you can still spot masons' marks, small signs each stonemason carved on his blocks so his work could be counted and paid.
Portugal's Romanesque churches are castles of faith: heavy granite, round arches and little light.

cards.text:
Portugal's oldest great churches are Romanesque, built mostly in the 12th and 13th centuries as the kingdom took shape. They have thick granite walls, round arches and small windows.

Cathedrals such as those of Lisbon, Porto and Coimbra look like castles, with battlements, because they were built in a time of war.

cards.title: Alcobaça

deep.x: The Cistercians, a reforming order shaped by Bernard of Clairvaux, preached poverty, work and plain buildings without figures or colour. At Alcobaça they ran huge estates, draining marshes and planting orchards, and the monastery became one of the richest in the kingdom.
A church of light and stone
Alcobaça is a hall church: its side aisles rise almost as high as the central nave, so light spreads evenly instead of falling in shafts. The effect is calm and very tall.
Pedro and Inês

Inês de Castro was a Galician noblewoman loved by the heir to the throne, Pedro. His father, Afonso IV, feared her family's influence, and in 1355 she was killed by royal courtiers. As king, Pedro took revenge on two of the killers. Their carved Gothic tombs face each other, so that, tradition says, they will see each other first when they rise on Judgement Day.
The kitchen
In the 18th century the monks built a vast tiled kitchen, with a channel of the river Alcoa running through it to bring fresh water and fish.

deep.w: Inês was crowned as a corpse in a real ceremony
deep.r: The coronation of her body is a legend with no contemporary evidence; Pedro did declare they had married in secret

deep.x: Alcobaça shows Cistercian Gothic at its purest: tall, bare and full of even light.

cards.text:
King Afonso Henriques gave Alcobaça to Cistercian monks in 1153. Its church, begun in 1178, was one of the first Gothic buildings in Portugal.

Its long, bare, white nave reflects Cistercian ideals of simplicity. Inside lie the carved tombs of King Pedro I and Inês de Castro, Portugal's most famous lovers.

cards.title: Batalha

deep.x: Work started in 1386 and went on in phases into the early 16th century, under several master builders, first Afonso Domingues and then a master called Huguet. The style blends local Gothic with touches of English Perpendicular, perhaps a nod to the queen, Philippa of Lancaster.
What to see
In the Founder's Chapel, João I and Philippa lie side by side, holding hands, surrounded by the tombs of their sons, including Henry the Navigator.
A daring vault

The chapter house is a square of about 19 metres whose star-shaped vault spans the whole room without support. Legend says it fell twice, and that the old, blind architect Afonso Domingues sat under it for three days after the scaffolding came down to prove it would stand. The writer Alexandre Herculano made the story famous in the 19th century.
The Unfinished Chapels

King Duarte planned a second pantheon: an octagon of chapels behind the church. Work stopped when Manuel I moved money and builders to the Jerónimos in Lisbon, leaving huge carved pillars rising towards a roof that was never built.
Since 1921 the chapter house has held the tomb of two unknown soldiers of the First World War, one from Flanders and one from Africa, with a permanent guard of honour.
Batalha is a battle won in stone: a royal vow turned into Portugal's finest Gothic building.

cards.text:
King João I promised a monastery to the Virgin Mary if he won the Battle of Aljubarrota in 1385. The result, Batalha ("battle"), took over a century to build and is a masterpiece of Portuguese Gothic.

Its chapter house has a vault about 19 metres wide with no central column, and its Unfinished Chapels are open to the sky.

cards.title: Manueline style

items: Cross of the Order of Christ

deep.x: The name is modern: the historian Francisco Adolfo de Varnhagen coined "Manueline" in 1842. Builders at the time simply mixed Gothic structures with ornament inspired by the sea, by royal emblems, and by Spanish, Flemish and Italian ideas.
Reading the symbols
The window of Tomar

The most famous Manueline window is in the Convent of Christ at Tomar, seat of the Order of Christ. Designed by Diogo de Arruda around 1510, it is framed by carved roots, ropes, coral, chains and buoys, crowned by the cross of the order and the royal arms. Some read it as a tree growing out of the sea, carrying the king's power.
Beyond the big monuments

x: The Church of Jesus in Setúbal (1490s), with columns twisted like ropes, is an early example
Manueline doors and windows appear on churches and houses in towns across the country
The 19th century revived the style as Neo-Manueline, as at Lisbon's Rossio station

deep.w: Manueline was a new way of building
deep.r: It was mostly decoration: the structures, plans and vaults underneath stayed Gothic

deep.x: Manueline is the Age of Discovery carved in stone: ropes, spheres and coral wrapped around Gothic bones.

cards.text:
Manueline is Portugal's own late Gothic style, from about 1490 to 1530, the age of King Manuel I. It covers doors, windows and columns with carved ropes, anchors, shells and coral.

It was paid for by the wealth of the sea route to India, and its decoration celebrates the voyages and the king's power.

cards.title: Jerónimos and Belém Tower

deep.x: Manuel I founded the Jerónimos near the chapel where Vasco da Gama's crew is said to have prayed before sailing for India in 1497. He gave it to the Hieronymite monks, who were to pray for the king and for sailors. A tax on the spice trade helped pay for it.
Two architects
Inside the church, slender columns open like palm trees into a wide vault that survived the 1755 earthquake. The two-storey cloister, carved in soft golden limestone, is one of the richest in Europe.
The tower in the river

The Belém Tower, by Francisco de Arruda, was built on a rock in the Tagus. Over the centuries the riverbank moved, and the tower now stands close to the shore. Its turrets show Moorish influence, which Arruda knew from his work on Portuguese forts in Morocco.
A small carved rhinoceros head under one turret is thought to show the animal sent from India to Manuel I in 1515, the first live rhino seen in Europe since Roman times.
Manuel I sent the rhino on to the Pope, but it drowned in a shipwreck in 1516; Albrecht Dürer made his famous woodcut without ever seeing it.
At Belém, the money and pride of the sea route to India became a monastery and a fortress.

cards.text:
On the riverbank at Belém stand Portugal's two most famous Manueline buildings. The Jerónimos Monastery, begun in 1501, holds the tombs of Vasco da Gama and Luís de Camões.

The Belém Tower, built about 1514–1519, guarded the entrance to Lisbon's harbour. Both have been World Heritage Sites since 1983.

cards.title: Tiled façades

deep.x: In Brazil's humid climate, tiles had proved a practical way to protect walls. Back in Portugal, rich returning emigrants built showy houses, and factories in Lisbon, Porto and Gaia turned out stencilled and printed patterns that ordinary owners could afford.
Great tiled walls
The entrance hall of Porto's São Bento station, decorated by Jorge Colaço between about 1905 and 1916, shows scenes of Portuguese history and country life in some 20,000 tiles.
Modern tiles

From the 1950s the painter Maria Keil designed abstract tile panels for the first Lisbon Metro stations, making tiles modern again. Later stations commissioned many leading artists, turning the metro into an underground gallery.
Saving them

Old tiles were often stolen from empty buildings and sold. Since 2007 the SOS Azulejo project, led by the Judiciary Police, has worked with museums and councils to register stolen tiles and prevent theft. Lisbon's rules now generally forbid removing tiles from building façades.
Tiles were valued on façades for practical reasons too: they shed rain, resist salty sea air and keep walls cooler in summer.
Azulejos turned Portuguese streets into galleries, and practical protection into decoration.

cards.text:
Azulejos moved from church interiors onto the outside of houses in the 19th century. Emigrants returning from Brazil, where tiled façades were common, are thought to have brought the fashion home, and factories made patterned tiles cheaply.

Tiles protect walls from rain and reflect light. Today whole streets in Lisbon, Porto, Aveiro and Ovar are wrapped in them.

cards.title: The Pombaline cage

deep.x: How the cage works

Plain masonry walls are strong when squeezed but crack and fall outwards when shaken sideways. The gaiola ties walls and floors together. Its key part is the frontal, an inner wall of upright and horizontal timbers braced with diagonal crosses and filled with brick or rubble.
Laboratory tests in Lisbon on rebuilt frontal walls confirm that they can bend a long way and absorb energy before they fail.
Weakened over time

x: Many ground floors were opened up for shops, cutting through the cage
Extra storeys were added on top, adding weight
Damp rotted timbers, and some were replaced with concrete

deep.x: A planned town

Vila Real de Santo António, on the Guadiana opposite Spain, was built from scratch by Pombal's government to control fishing and the border. Its grid of streets and its central square repeat the ideas of the Baixa, and some of the stone was cut in Lisbon and shipped south.
The diagonal braces are called cruzes de Santo André, after the X-shaped cross on which Saint Andrew is said to have died.
The gaiola pombalina made buildings flexible and tied together, an idea modern seismic design still follows.

cards.text:
After the 1755 earthquake, Lisbon's Baixa was rebuilt with the gaiola pombalina, a timber cage hidden inside masonry walls. Its diagonal braces help a building sway rather than burst apart.

The same planning ideas created a whole new town, Vila Real de Santo António in the Algarve, laid out from 1774.

cards.title: Estado Novo buildings

deep.x: In the 1930s, the public works minister Duarte Pacheco commissioned strongly modernist buildings, such as the Instituto Superior Técnico in Lisbon by Porfírio Pardal Monteiro. From the late 1930s taste shifted towards a nationalist look, with pitched tiled roofs, stone arcades and towers.
Building the nation
The 1940 exhibition

The Exposição do Mundo Português in Belém celebrated 800 years since the founding of Portugal and 300 since independence was restored in 1640. Its temporary pavilions shaped the Belém riverfront, including the gardens of Praça do Império. The Padrão was first built for it in light materials, then rebuilt in concrete and stone in 1960.
A survey that surprised

In the 1950s, teams of architects travelled the country for the Survey of Popular Architecture in Portugal, published in 1961. The regime hoped they would find one typical "Portuguese house". Instead they found huge regional variety and practical, almost modern logic, which inspired a new generation, including Fernando Távora and the Porto School.

deep.w: The regime built only traditional-looking buildings
deep.r: Many Estado Novo works, from hospitals to dams and the Técnico, were strongly modernist

deep.x: Estado Novo architecture mixed modern engineering with a carefully staged national look.

cards.text:
The Estado Novo dictatorship (1933–1974) used architecture to project order and national pride. After an early modernist phase, it favoured a "Português Suave" style that dressed modern structures in traditional roofs, arches and stone.

Its legacy includes courthouses, schools, housing estates, the Padrão dos Descobrimentos and the bridge over the Tagus, now called 25 de Abril.

cards.title: Siza and Souto de Moura

deep.x: Siza

Siza's tidal pools at Leça da Palmeira sit among the rocks by the sea, so that concrete walls and natural stone frame the Atlantic. After the 1988 fire in Lisbon's Chiado, he led its reconstruction, keeping the old façades. His Portugal Pavilion for Expo '98 has a thin concrete canopy, about 20 cm thick, that hangs like a sheet between two porticos.
Souto de Moura

He worked with Siza before opening his own office. His Braga Municipal Stadium (2003), built for Euro 2004, has only two stands; at one end the rock face of an old quarry closes the pitch. The Casa das Histórias Paula Rego in Cascais (2009) has two red concrete towers shaped like pyramids. He also led the design of the Porto Metro's stations.
Together
In 2005 they designed the Serpentine Gallery Pavilion in London together, and their offices share a building in Porto.
The Leça tidal pools and Siza's nearby Boa Nova Tea House were classified as National Monuments in 2011, a rare honour for works by a living architect.
The Porto School proved that modern architecture can be local, quiet and exact.

cards.text:
Álvaro Siza (born 1933) and Eduardo Souto de Moura (born 1952) both won the Pritzker Prize, in 1992 and 2011. Both came from the "Porto School", shaped by Fernando Távora.

Their buildings are calm, precise and shaped by their sites: pools set among sea rocks, a stadium cut into a quarry, white walls that frame the light.

cards.title: Calçada portuguesa

deep.x: The stones

Lisbon's white limestone traditionally comes from quarries in the limestone hills of Estremadura, north of the city, and the black basalt from the ancient volcanic rocks of the Lisbon area. Elsewhere local stone is used, such as granite in the north, with red or pink stones for colour.
A craft of the knees

A calceteiro works kneeling, sets each stone by eye and taps it into the sand with a small hammer, using string lines for levels and templates for patterns. Joints are filled with sand and the surface is compacted. A good pavement can last for decades, and single stones are easy to replace.
The debate

Falls on polished, wet calçada are common, especially on steep streets, and uneven surfaces are hard for wheelchairs, prams and older people. Lisbon's plans have replaced some stretches with smoother stone slabs, while keeping artistic calçada in squares and historic areas. Supporters argue that rougher stones and good laying reduce the risk.
Calçada in the world

deep.w: Calçada is a medieval tradition
deep.r: Stone paving is ancient, but decorative black-and-white calçada began in Lisbon only in the 1840s

deep.x: Calçada is heritage you walk on, and keeping it means balancing beauty, safety and skilled hands.

cards.text:
Portuguese pavement is still laid by hand, stone by stone, by craftsmen called calceteiros. White limestone and black basalt are cut into small cubes and set in sand to make waves, stars and ships.

In 2021 the craft was added to Portugal's national inventory of intangible heritage. But it is slippery when wet, and cities debate where to keep it.

quiz.q: Which king gives the Manueline style its name?
quiz.explain: Manuel I reigned from 1495 to 1521.

quiz.q: Whose tombs face each other at Alcobaça?
options: Pedro I and Inês de Castro
quiz.explain: Tradition says they will see each other first on Judgement Day.

quiz.q: What is the gaiola pombalina?
quiz.explain: It ties walls and floors so buildings sway instead of collapsing.

quiz.q: Which Portuguese architect won the Pritzker Prize in 2011?
quiz.explain: Siza won it in 1992.

lessons.title: Portuguese science and invention
lessons.summary: From navigators' instruments to modern labs: Portugal's scientists and what they discovered.

cards.title: Science for the sea
